title: Run JoinDependentFilterRule before DistributivityRule
hypothesis: In q19 the whole OR-of-ANDs predicate is evaluated in a FILTER above the lineitem⋈part HASH_JOIN (0.42s). The join emits 2.14M rows (0.68s), but only 1,170 survive. JoinDependentFilterRule derives per-table OR filters (for example (p_brand='Brand#45' AND ...) OR (...) on part, and the l_quantity range OR on lineitem). It only fires on a root OR, though. DistributivityRule is registered earlier (optimizer.cpp:52 vs :69) and factors the common p_partkey=l_partkey term out first, so the root becomes an AND and nothing is derived. A previous evolve run measured the reordered version: q19 336->157ms (-53%), join output 2.14M->2.7K rows.
plan: In src/optimizer/optimizer.cpp, move `rewriter.rules.push_back(make_uniq<JoinDependentFilterRule>(rewriter));` (line 69) to just before the DistributivityRule push_back (line 52). Nothing else changes. Check that the q19 plan now shows derived filters on the part scan and the lineitem side, and that the result is unchanged. Run the unit tests for the optimizer and filter pushdown (test/optimizer/*, any test that mentions join_dependent).
expected_gain: q19 -40..-55%, so roughly -4..-5% on the visible geomean. It may also help other disjunctive join predicates in hidden templates (TPC-H q07-style nation pairs).
generality: Applies to any WHERE clause written as an OR of conjunctions that each touch several tables and repeat a join key, which is common in BI-generated SQL and in TPC-H q07/q19 patterns. The derived filters are redundant and implied, so correctness holds. The worst case is a little extra evaluation of the derived OR filters when they are not selective.
risk: Low. Only the rule order changes. The expression rewriter runs the rules to a fixpoint, so Distributivity still runs afterwards. Check that no infinite rewrite loop appears (derived filters must not be re-derived) and that no plan-snapshot tests break.

title: Length-aware selectivity for contains()/LIKE scan filters
hypothesis: q09 (1284ms, the largest template) has p_name LIKE '%ghost%', which becomes contains(). Cardinality estimation gives this expression filter the default 0.2 selectivity, so the join order is poor. The plan shows two hash joins of about 2.6s each, on 3.27M rows. A previous run measured a length-aware estimate, sel = max(0.2*0.75^L, 0.01) in InspectTableFilter (relation_statistics_helper.cpp, EXPRESSION_FILTER case): q09 -35%.
plan: In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, InspectTableFilter: for an ExpressionFilter whose expression is a contains/like function with a constant pattern, estimate selectivity from the literal length as above. Verify the function names in that file first.
expected_gain: q09 -30% (about -2.5% geomean)
generality: Any substring filter on a dimension table feeding a join order. It could misorder joins when a short literal is very common.
risk: Medium. It changes join orders in other queries that use LIKE filters.

title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins
hypothesis: q13's RIGHT HASH_JOIN (o_custkey=c_custkey; build side is customer, 1.5M dense keys) takes 1.76s, and the agg on top takes 2.21s. A perfect HJ is not used for RIGHT joins. A previous run found 3 gates (optimizer min/max propagation and an off-by-one duplicate check) and measured q13 -20%.
plan: Investigate the PerfectHashJoinExecutor eligibility checks in physical_hash_join.cpp / perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp and in the join-stats propagation in the optimizer. Allow RIGHT/outer joins with dense unique build keys.
generality: FK joins against dense-key dimension tables with outer semantics.
risk: Medium. Needs correct RIGHT-join match tracking.

title: Length-aware selectivity for contains()/LIKE scan filters v2
hypothesis: q09 is the slowest template at about 1284ms. Its p_name LIKE '%x%' becomes contains() and is pushed into the scan as an EXPRESSION_FILTER. RelationStatisticsHelper::InspectTableFilter (relation_statistics_helper.cpp:446) handles only CONJUNCTION_AND and CONSTANT_COMPARISON. Any other filter falls through, so ExtractGetStats at line 147 applies the flat DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY of 0.2. That overestimate gives a bad join order: two hash joins of about 2.6s each on 3.27M rows. A previous run measured q09 -35% with this exact mechanism.
plan: In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, InspectTableFilter: add a TableFilterType::EXPRESSION_FILTER case. Cast to ExpressionFilter and look at filter.expr. If it is a BoundFunctionExpression named contains, like_escape, ~~ (like) or prefix/suffix, and one argument is a constant VARCHAR (BoundConstantExpression), let L be the literal length with % and _ excluded. Then sel = max(0.2*0.75^L, 0.01) and the result is max(1, cardinality*sel). Also descend into CONJUNCTION_AND as today, and into OPTIONAL_FILTER if it wraps one. The has_equality_filter check at line 146 compares against base_table_cardinality, so a lower estimate naturally overrides the 0.2 default. Check the exact function names with Grep (contains, ~~, like_escape) before coding. Verify the q09 plan flips by running profile q09.m0, and check that the results match.
expected_gain: q09 -30% (about -2.5% visible geomean). Other templates with LIKE filters on dimension tables could improve slightly (q16/q13 use NOT LIKE, which this should leave alone).
generality: Any query with a substring/LIKE predicate on a table feeding join ordering, which is common in analytics. It could underestimate a short, very common literal. The 0.01 floor and the 0.75^L decay keep 1-2 character literals at 0.11-0.15 selectivity.
risk: Medium-low. It changes only estimates, never results. Join orders could flip on hidden queries with LIKE. Negated forms (NOT LIKE) must be excluded.

title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins v2 (all 3 gates)
hypothesis: q13 is now the largest template (785.6ms, 17.1% of total). Its plan is customer LEFT JOIN orders, run as a RIGHT HASH_JOIN with customer (1.5M dense unique c_custkey) as the build side. That join took about 1.8s CPU. The perfect HJ is never used here, because of three gates I verified in the code: (1) perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:73 requires join_type==INNER. (2) join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:275 computes compute_aggregates_anyway only for INNER joins. The probe keys sit behind a compress projection, so probe_info is empty and the join gets no build min/max. (3) perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:115 bails when ht.Count() > build_range. A fully dense key set has range+1 keys, so this off-by-one rejects every fully dense build, including INNER ones. A previous run fixed all three and measured q13 -20% (join operator 1.87s→0.19s CPU).
plan: 1) In src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp near line 275, allow compute_aggregates_anyway for RIGHT joins too, as well as INNER. Single condition, equality, same conditions as today. 2) In src/execution/operator/join/perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp: (a) CanDoPerfectHashJoin at line 73 should accept JoinType::RIGHT alongside INNER. (b) Fix the dup check at line 115 to `ht.Count() > build_range + 1`. (c) RIGHT builds keep NULL-key rows in the HT with has_null=false, so the build fill must check key validity and skip NULL keys. Those rows still have to be emitted by the RIGHT scan as unmatched. (d) Track RIGHT-join matches. Mark found_match in a per-slot byte array during probe, then flush it into the HT rows' found_match field before the outer scan (PrepareScanHT / the full-outer scan path in physical_hash_join.cpp). The previous run measured this at -17.8%, against -11.6% for writing found_match into rows directly at probe time. Make sure the existing RIGHT-join outer-scan code in physical_hash_join.cpp still emits unmatched build rows. Keep MAX_BUILD_SIZE as it is.
expected_gain: q13 -15..-20% (about -1.5% geomean). Fixing the off-by-one may also help INNER joins on fully dense dimension keys in q02, q05 and q08 (nation, region, supplier).
generality: FK joins against dense-key dimension tables with outer semantics (LEFT JOIN fact-to-dim, or dim-to-fact planned as RIGHT). Fully dense INNER builds also gain from the off-by-one fix. Downside: a sparse range close to MAX_BUILD_SIZE could cost more memory, but the existing range cap still applies.
risk: Medium. RIGHT-join correctness for unmatched rows and NULL build keys is the main risk; bench results checks should catch it. The optimizer change only adds min/max aggregate computation for RIGHT joins.

title: Substring prefilter over contiguous string runs for LIKE/contains scan filters
hypothesis: In q13 (648ms, 14.5% of the total) the orders TABLE_SCAN with the filter o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%' takes 2.60s of CPU, the largest single operator in the profile. The join and the aggregate above it are now cheap after E0003. The ExpressionFilter is evaluated per row through the generic LIKE matcher. FSST decode with enable_fsst_vectors=false writes the strings back to back into one buffer, so a whole run of rows can be checked for the literal with one SIMD search. A previous run measured q13 -11% with this mechanism.
plan: In src/storage/table/column_data.cpp, ColumnData::Filter (line 348): after Scan, if the filter is an EXPRESSION_FILTER whose expression is ~~ / !~~ / contains (or NOT of these) with a constant pattern that uses only '%' wildcards (no '_' or escape), extract the longest literal segment of at least 2 bytes. For a FLAT VARCHAR result, walk the rows and group the non-inlined strings whose data pointer equals the previous string's end into runs. Search each run with an SSE2 first+last-byte candidate scan and memcmp to confirm. Keep the scan block overlapping into the run tail; do not finish the tail with a scalar loop, because the prior run found that removes the gain. Map each hit back to its row (a hit must lie fully inside one string). Rows without the literal are decided directly: false for positive LIKE, true for NOT LIKE. Only candidate rows go through the original ColumnSegment::FilterSelection / expression, with a reduced selection. Inlined (<=12 byte) strings and non-contiguous strings fall back to the per-row path. Do not depend on FSST_VECTOR: it never reaches this path.
expected_gain: q13 -10% (prior run -11%). Smaller gains for any other LIKE/contains scan filter (q09 p_name LIKE '%ghost%' on part, a small table).
generality: Any substring-style LIKE/contains/NOT LIKE scan filter on VARCHAR columns, which are common in analytics (comments, names). Columns with short inlined strings fall back and so do not slow down. If almost every row matches the literal (no pruning), the extra pass adds a small overhead.
risk: Medium. Correctness depends on NOT semantics, NULL handling (NULL rows must still be filtered out) and matches that cross a string boundary. The implementer should check results with dbe-tool sql against an equivalent filter that blocks pushdown (e.g. concat(o_comment,'') NOT LIKE ...).

title: Join key-set range filter through compress projections
hypothesis: q18 (695ms, 15.5%) scans all 59,986,052 lineitem rows for the l_orderkey = o_orderkey join, while only 111 orderkeys survive the HAVING semi join. The join filter pushdown cannot pass through __internal_compress_integral projections, and a single min/max range over random keys prunes nothing. A prior run (offset-aware pushdown plus an OptionalFilter OR of up to threshold ranges split at the largest gaps) measured q18 -13.6%, with lineitem scan rows going 60M→17.5M.
plan: In src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp, follow column bindings through compress-integral projections and record the storage offset in JoinFilterPushdownColumn. In src/execution/operator/join/join_filter_pushdown.cpp (and wherever the min/max filters are built in physical_hash_join.cpp), when the build has few distinct keys (threshold < n <= 64*threshold), build an OptionalFilter holding an OR of ranges split at the largest gaps, with the offset added.
generality: Selective joins against large fact tables whose keys are clustered by row group, and pushdown through compressed materialization in general.
risk: Medium. Offsets must be applied correctly, but the filters are optional (zonemap only), so a wrong pruning decision is the main risk.

title: Bloom filter on first key of multi-key hash joins
hypothesis: In q09 (799ms, the largest template) the lineitem-partsupp join has 2 keys (ps_suppkey, ps_partkey). CanUseBloomFilter requires conditions.size()==1, so this join gets no BF. A prior run measured q09 -21% by building the BF on key 0 only.
plan: In src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp InsertHashes, gather join key column 0 and hash it on its own for the BF. In physical_hash_join.cpp CanUseBloomFilter / FinalizeFilters, allow multiple conditions and push the BF only for the filter on join_condition 0.
generality: Composite-key FK joins (partsupp-style bridge tables).
risk: Medium. The BF hash has to match the probe-side hashing.

title: Join min/max + BF pushdown through CM compress projections (q09)
hypothesis: In q09 the orders scan reads all 15M rows for the o_orderkey hash join, because the join filter pushdown stops at __internal_compress_integral_* projections that compressed materialization inserts. A prior run measured: offset-aware min/max (+off) and BF (hash of (x-off) masked to key width) cut the orders scan from 15M to 2.96M rows, q09 -8.2%. The current best now has BF on the first key of multi-key HJ (E0005), so more joins in q09 have a BF to push.
plan: In src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp, follow bindings through projections whose expression is __internal_compress_integral_*(col, const_offset), and record the offset in JoinFilterPushdownColumn (join_filter_pushdown.hpp). In physical_hash_join.cpp (JoinFilterPushdownInfo::FinalizeFilters / PushBloomFilter), add the offset to min/max constants, and for the BF hash the probe value the way the build side does. Simplest: only push the BF when the build key is itself the compressed value, or skip the BF when offset != 0, and push min/max only. TopN optimizer and RowGroupPruner also call GetPushdownFilterTargets, so they must reject columns with an offset. If the q18 key-set issue landed first, reuse its offset plumbing.
expected_gain: q09 -8% (prior), possibly q05/q07/q08 a few %
generality: Any join whose probe key passes through a compressed-materialization projection, which is common whenever an aggregate or sort sits between the scan and the join.
risk: Medium. An offset applied wrongly causes wrong pruning, so test with an offset-shifted key range against a col+0 variant.

title: Exact key-bitmap mode for join Bloom filter on dense integer build keys
hypothesis: Join BFs are hashed and approximate (sector-blocked BloomFilter in bloom_filter.hpp). Each probe pays a hash plus a lookup and still passes false positives through to the hash join. Dense integer FK keys (partkey, suppkey, orderkey, custkey) are common. When max-min of the build keys is at most about 128*build_count, one bit per key value gives an exact filter at similar memory, with no hashing and no false positives. A previous run on this workload measured -9.5..-12.4% on q09 (lineitem scan CPU 5.28→4.55s, rows exactly 3.27M), -10.5..-11.5% on q16, and -15% on q21 (l2/l3 scans 0.83/1.06s → 0.38/0.53s). The cap had to be 128 bits/key; at 64, the q21 delim BFs stayed hashed and the gain was only -4.9%. The current best (E0005) now builds BFs on the first key of multi-key HJs, so more joins benefit.
plan: 1) BloomFilter (src/include/duckdb/planner/filter/bloom_filter.hpp, src/planner/filter/bloom_filter.cpp): add an exact mode: SetExactRange(min, range) allocates ceil(range/64) uint64 words; InsertKeys/LookupKeys work on raw integer values (v - min), and values outside the range miss. 2) In JoinFilterPushdownInfo::FinalizeFilters / PushBloomFilter (src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp), decide exact mode from the raw final min/max. Gate: a single equality condition that is a BF candidate, NULLs not equal, left type == right type, 8..64-bit integer key, no storage_offset on the pushdown column (keep the existing rule that offset columns get no BF), and range < min(2^32, 128*ht.Count()). 3) Fill it: in JoinHashTable::Finalize (join_hashtable.cpp, next to InsertFirstKeyIntoBloomFilter), when the BF is in exact mode, read key column 0 from the row layout and set the bits instead of hashing. Bits must be set atomically, or per-thread with an OR, if the fill is parallel. 4) Probe: in BFTableFilter::Filter, take the exact path that skips HashInternal. Use UnifiedVectorFormat, and slice first if sel is set and the vector is not flat (SEQUENCE vectors). FilterValue handles exact mode too. In CheckStatistics, prune by range overlap, but never return ALWAYS_FALSE when NULLs pass. 5) Keep the hashed path unchanged for everything else. Verify correctness against SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown' on TEMP tables, including keys at min/max boundaries, negative keys, and INNER vs IS NOT DISTINCT FROM.
expected_gain: q09 -10%, q16 -10%, q21 -10..-15% (prior measurements), and possibly q05/q07/q08 a few %. Geomean about -3..-4%.
generality: Any hash join on a dense integer key (surrogate or FK keys, the dominant pattern in star/snowflake schemas) whose probe side is a scan that can take a pushed BF. Queries with sparse keys keep the hashed BF and are unaffected. A small slowdown is possible when the bitmap (up to 128 bits/key) exceeds cache where the hashed BF fit, but the cap keeps it at most the pointer table size.
risk: Medium. Off-by-one errors at range boundaries, mishandled sel or SEQUENCE/constant vectors, or a statistics prune that returns ALWAYS_FALSE incorrectly would produce wrong results. The gate and tests above cover these.

title: Exact bitmap BF through CM compress offset
hypothesis: E0006 records JoinFilterPushdownColumn::storage_offset when the probe key passes through __internal_compress_integral_*(x, off). Only offset-shifted min/max and range-set filters are pushed. The BF is explicitly skipped (physical_hash_join.cpp:1059 requires storage_offset.IsNull() and !has_cast). As a result the q09 orders scan still reads all 15M rows into the o_orderkey HJ. A previous run on the same workload pushed the EXACT bitmap BF through the offset: orders scan 15M→2.94M rows, q09 -14.3%. The hashed-BF version was +4.7%, so only the exact mode is worth porting. E0007 has since landed the exact bitmap (BloomFilter::SetExactRange/LookupExact), so the remaining piece is a probe-side shift.
plan: 1) In bloom_filter.hpp BFTableFilter, add a uint64_t key_offset (wrapping add, default 0). It applies only in exact mode: the probe computes LookupExact(widen(stored_value) - offset_as_u64), with signed or unsigned widening based on the scanned (storage) column type, not the HT key type. Apply the same shift in FilterValue and CheckStatistics, which shifts the zonemap min/max with overflow checks; if unsure, return NO_PRUNING_POSSIBLE. Include it in Equals/Copy/ToString/serialization if those exist. 2) In physical_hash_join.cpp FinalizeFilters (~l.1057-1067), add a second branch: when storage_offset is not NULL, ht, key 0, CanUseBloomFilter, and the exact gate (TrySetExactBloomFilter) succeeds, defer the push and pass the offset. The compressed key type (condition type) differs from storage_type, so allow has_cast in this branch only, because the scan column is the original integer column. In PushBloomFilter (deferred path), only push if bf->IsExact() && !ExactOverflow() and set key_offset; otherwise push nothing (never hashed BF through an offset). The exact gate must be decided before Finalize fills the bitmap; if it fails, don't build the BF. 3) Verify on TEMP tables against SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown': a BIGINT key with a non-zero min (e.g. 1e9+k), negative keys, an aggregate between scan and join so CM fires, and a sparse build (~10%) so the selectivity wrapper keeps the filter; check in EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the probe scan row count drops.
expected_gain: q09 -10..-14% (prior -14.3%); possibly q05/q07/q08/q18 a few % wherever CM sits between scan and join.
generality: Any join on dense integer keys whose probe key passes through compressed materialization (aggregates or sorts between scan and join), which is common in star/FK joins. Little regression risk: the SelectivityOptionalFilter wrapper disables it when it is unselective.
risk: Medium. A wrong offset sign or widening silently drops rows (wrong results). Mitigate with the offset-shifted key tests above. CheckStatistics shifting must not over-prune.

title: Large perfect hash aggregate (up to 22 bits) with parallel combine and source
hypothesis: In q13 (644ms, 16% of total) the inner HASH_GROUP_BY on c_custkey (1.5M dense groups, stats range 1..1.5M which is about 21 bits) takes 2.13s CPU, the largest operator in the plan. CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (plan_aggregate.cpp:127) rejects it because the total bits exceed perfect_ht_threshold, so it falls back to the radix HT with hashing, probing and partitioned finalize. A previous run on this codebase measured q13 -18.6% (706->576ms) and, re-implemented on top of the RIGHT perfect-HJ base, q13 -24.5% (646->488ms). In that run the larger threshold alone gave only -3.6%, because PerfectAggregateHashTable Combine and the PhysicalPerfectHashAggregate source were serial over 2M slots, which also made the downstream pipeline single-threaded. Both had to be parallelised.
plan: 1) plan_aggregate.cpp CanUsePerfectHashAggregate: allow total bits up to 22 when (a) the estimated input cardinality >= slots/2 (dense enough), and (b) slots * tuple_size * (threads+1) <= max_memory/8. Otherwise keep the existing perfect_ht_threshold rule. 2) perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp Combine: let several threads combine their local tables into the global one at the same time, using striped locks over slot ranges (for example 64 stripes) instead of one global lock. Combine aggregate states using the source (local) arena allocator, then move it into the global table (TakeAllocator) under the global lock. 3) physical_perfecthash_aggregate.cpp source: make GetData parallel. Global source state hands out blocks of slots through an atomic cursor, each thread scans its block, and MaxThreads returns slots/block_size. Check that ScanAll can start at a given offset (or add a range scan). Keep the result order unspecified, as with hash agg.
expected_gain: q13 -18..-25% (about -1.5% geomean). Possibly other group-bys on dense integer keys with 2^16..2^22 range (custkey/partkey/suppkey-style keys).
generality: Any GROUP BY on one or more integer columns whose combined stats range is up to 4M slots and dense relative to the input, such as FK-keyed aggregates after joins. Risk of slowdown: a sparse range with a small input, which the density guard prevents. Also many threads each allocating a 4M-slot local table, which the memory guard limits.
risk: Medium. The parallel combine must be race-free (stripes must be disjoint slot ranges, and the allocator move must happen under the lock). The source change must cover every slot exactly once. Test against SET perfect_ht_threshold=0 / disabled perfect agg, and compare count/sum/min/max/string aggregates and NULL groups on TEMP tables with 1-4M dense keys.

title: Distinct HT partitioned on group hash
hypothesis: q16 does count(DISTINCT ps_suppkey) GROUP BY brand,type,size, with about 64K estimated groups. The distinct radix HT partitions on hash(G,x), so every distinct partition holds pieces of every group. Distinct finalize then re-sinks each partition into the main HT, and each task touches nearly all groups. That is a large re-aggregation plus a combine. A prior run on this codebase spliced hash(G) into the radix bits [36,48) of the distinct HT hash and measured q16 -12..-13% twice, and -11% on a later re-implementation.
plan: In radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp/.hpp add a member (e.g. partition_prefix_count = number of leading group columns) on RadixPartitionedHashTable. In Sink, when it is set, hash the full key, compute hash(first prefix cols), and replace bits [36,48) (the RadixPartitioning MAX_RADIX_BITS mask region) with those bits of the group hash. Call a pre-hashed AddChunk overload and keep the sink_count update inside it, so the adaptivity logic still fires. In physical_hash_aggregate.cpp, when distinct radix tables are built for a grouped aggregate with estimated_cardinality >= 4096, set the prefix count to the number of main group columns, and skip TryAddCompressedGroups in that mode. Distinct finalize is unchanged: each partition now holds whole groups.
expected_gain: q16 -10..-13%. Other count(DISTINCT) GROUP BY templates gain a few %.
generality: Any grouped aggregate with DISTINCT aggregates over many groups. Ungrouped DISTINCT is unaffected (gated). A skewed group could unbalance partitions, and low-group-count queries are gated off by the estimate.
risk: Medium-low. The hash only affects partitioning, so correctness holds as long as the same hash is used consistently for equality probing in the distinct HT: the full hash still decides the slot, only the radix bits are replaced. Test spilling with a low memory_limit.

title: Semi-join RHS-aware estimate + HAVING selectivity
hypothesis: q18 IN (SELECT l_orderkey ... GROUP BY HAVING sum>300): the SEMI case in CardinalityEstimator::CalculateUpdatedDenom (cardinality_estimator.cpp:268) uses left.denom*5 and ignores the RHS size, and relation_manager gives the HAVING filter no selectivity. The optimizer therefore over-estimates the orders⋈subquery result and keeps customer on the build side. A prior run measured q18 -7..-8% with both changes, and either alone did nothing.
plan: cardinality_estimator.cpp CalculateUpdatedDenom SEMI: use selectivity = max(DEFAULT_SEMI_ANTI_SELECTIVITY, tdom/rhs_cardinality). In relation_manager.cpp (near l.495), apply an extra 0.2 to the estimate of an aggregate relation that has a HAVING (filter over aggregate) above it. Verify with EXPLAIN that q18's customer join flips.
generality: IN/EXISTS subqueries with selective RHS (HAVING, filters). Other join orders can change, so check q04/q21/q20-like semi joins.
risk: Medium: it changes join orders broadly for semi joins.

title: OR-of-ranges scan filter as dense-mask ExpressionFilter
hypothesis: q19 (190ms) now has per-table OR filters, derived by E0001's JoinDependentFilter, on lineitem/part (for example OR of l_quantity BETWEEN ranges). These filters are evaluated as generic ExpressionFilters through the expression executor with a selection vector, which costs a lot per row. A prior run measured q19 -7..-11% from evaluating OR-of-range conjunctions as a dense mask over the full vector and then gathering into the selection.
plan: In the ExpressionFilter scan path (src/planner/filter/expression_filter.cpp, and the place in ColumnSegment/ColumnData where expression filters are applied), detect when the expression is an OR of comparisons/BETWEENs on the filtered column against constants. When the incoming selection is sparse or full, evaluate the ranges branch-free over the dense vector into a bitmask, then build the output selection from the mask. Fall back to the existing path otherwise.
expected_gain: q19 -7..-11% (prior run); small gains for other OR-range filters
generality: Any scan with an OR of range/equality predicates on one column (IN-ranges, bucketed filters). It could be slightly slower on tiny vectors with very sparse selections, which the gather handles.
risk: Low-medium. Contained in the filter evaluation path; correctness of NULL handling must be checked.

title: FSST batched decode + substring prefilter bundle (q13)
hypothesis: q13 (~638ms, 2nd largest) spends its scan time decoding FSST o_comment strings one at a time and then evaluating NOT LIKE '%special%requests%'. Two prior measurements: FSST batched decode (one shared allocation, remaining-space bound, used only via DecompressVector) gave q13 -4..-7%; the substring prefilter over contiguous decoded runs (E0004) gave -7.7%. Each alone is under q13's ~14% noise bar. Combined they should be about -12..-15%.
plan: 1) In src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp, in the scan/DecompressVector path, decode a whole vector's strings into one shared string-heap buffer, bounding writes by the remaining space instead of a per-string worst case. 2) Re-apply the E0004 approach in ColumnData::Filter / ColumnSegment::FilterSelection: for a contains/LIKE ExpressionFilter with a constant literal, search the literal over back-to-back decoded strings with memchr/memmem, and map each hit to its row. Keep the fallback for all other cases.
expected_gain: q13 -12..-15%; small gains on other templates with LIKE over FSST columns (q09 p_name, q16 s_comment)
generality: Any scan of FSST-compressed strings, and any substring filter on string columns.
risk: Medium: string lifetime and heap ownership in the batched decode, and NULL/empty-string handling in the prefilter.

title: Large perfect HA v2: large-mode-only code paths, plan-identical guard for other templates
hypothesis: q13 is the largest template (646ms, 16.6%). Its inner HASH_GROUP_BY on c_custkey (1.5M dense groups, 15M input rows) takes 2.40s CPU, the largest single operator in the profile. E0009 (perfect HA up to 22 bits, striped parallel combine, parallel source, lazy slot init, DELIM_SCAN guard) gave a consistent q13 -20..-23% over 3 runs. It was retired because the official bench showed q16 +14% and q18 +7.8%. Neither template should be able to reach the large mode: q16 groups by VARCHARs, q18's outer agg groups by VARCHAR c_name, and its IN-subquery agg on l_orderkey needs about 26 bits, which is more than 22. So the regressions were either noise or overhead that E0009 added to code shared by ALL perfect HAs, such as the refactored Combine (CombineRange/TakeAllocator) and the ScanRange source. Keeping the original code path for every non-large perfect HA, and confirming that the q16/q18 plans are unchanged, removes the second possibility.

title: Stop compressing hash-join keys in compressed materialization
hypothesis: Compressed materialization (CM) compresses both join-key columns of a single-condition comparison join. CompressComparisonJoin puts the probe key in probe_compress_bindings, which inserts __internal_compress_integral_* projections on the probe side. Those projections block the Bloom-filter pushdown into the probe scan. E0006 only plumbed min/max and key-set ranges through them, and E0008, which pushed the BF through, was retired. They also add decompress/compress pairs (q13: a 0.21s CPU decompress projection on 15M rows, then a compress). Measured on the current best with SET disabled_optimizers='compressed_materialization', JSON profile of raw q09: latency 542→335ms, CPU 3.69→2.21s. The o_orderkey=l_orderkey join drops from 1.60s to 0.73s because the orders probe scan now gets the BF and emits 2.94M rows instead of 15M. The lineitem/part join also drops from 0.54s to 0.41s, and the 0.12s compress projection disappears. Alternating warm runs of the raw query: q09 ~484→~418ms (-14%), q03 ~204→~179ms (-12%). q13, q18 and q05 were unchanged within noise. That is the whole-CM upper bound; join keys are the part that blocks the BF.
plan: In src/optimizer/compressed_materialization/compress_comparison_join.cpp, CompressedMaterialization::CompressComparisonJoin: remove (or gate off) the block at lines ~57-85 that compresses both join-condition columns generically and adds lhs_colref.binding to probe_compress_bindings. Every condition then goes through GetReferencedBindings, so key columns are never compressed. Build-side payload columns are still compressed, and the probe side is still left alone. UpdateComparisonJoinStats then has nothing to update for the keys, which is fine. Step 1: measure raw q09 and q03, not wrapped in count(*), because the wrapper changes the plan. Alternate runs with and without the change. Discard the first 2-3 runs of each dbe-tool sql process, because warm-up made a false -30% on q05. Step 2: if the key-only variant gets clearly less than SET disabled_optimizers='compressed_materialization' gives on q09/q03, try variant B: return early from CompressComparisonJoin (no join CM at all; aggregate/order/distinct CM unchanged). Keep whichever is faster across the full bench. Check that EXPLAIN for q09 shows the BF on the orders scan and that q13 still uses the perfect RIGHT hash join (its keys become BIGINT instead of UINTEGER).
expected_gain: q09 -10..-14%, q03 -8..-12%; possibly q05/q07/q08 and q13 (no decompress/compress pair) a few %. Geomean about -2%.
generality: Helps any join whose probe key would have been compressed by CM: integer FK joins where the build side is large enough to pass the CM thresholds. Removing the key projections lets the runtime BF, min/max and perfect-HJ filters reach the probe scan directly, and saves a projection per key. Could get slower: joins with very large builds, where 4-byte compressed keys made the hash table smaller and more cache-friendly, and memory-bound or spilling joins. The payload compression that matters most for memory is kept.
risk: Low-medium. The change only removes an optimization, so correctness risk is minimal: uncompressed keys go through the same code path as joins below the CM thresholds. The main risk is performance on large-build joins without a selective BF, and the perfect HJ / exact-BF gates seeing BIGINT keys instead of compressed ones; check q13 and q18.

title: Deliminate selective-LHS SEMI delim joins with simple RHS + join filters for RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI

title: Exact-bitmap BF pushed through CM compress offset
hypothesis: FinalizeFilters (physical_hash_join.cpp:1059) builds a BF only when pushdown_column.storage_offset.IsNull() && !has_cast. When compressed materialization compresses a join key (__internal_compress_integral_*(x, off)), the probe scan gets min/max only. Call TrySetExactBloomFilter with the RAW (compressed, unshifted) min/max of the HT keys, not the offset-shifted values used for the min/max filters. Keep every other guard unchanged (one delim get, one join, INNER/SEMI child join with only colref = colref conditions, SubqueryIsSimple RHS). Optimize() then removes the join with the DelimGet. RemoveJoinWithDelimGet adds IS NOT NULL on the replacing columns. ConvertNotDistinctToEqual turns NDF into = when the RHS column is non-null, so the join filters can be generated (NDF conditions are skipped in JoinFilterPushdownOptimizer::GenerateJoinFilters). Before relying on the NDF->= conversion for ANTI, check semantics: an LHS row with a NULL key must still be emitted, both in ANTI (probe side LHS) and in RIGHT_ANTI (build side LHS, emitted by the unmatched-build scan). Check how JoinHashTable handles NULL build keys for RIGHT_ANTI (null_values_are_equal / the build-side null filtering in join_hashtable.cpp). If NULL build keys are dropped for RIGHT_ANTI, do not convert to = for ANTI; it may then need an explicit IS NOT NULL OR ... rewrite, or just skip the conversion and accept no BF. Tests: (1) a temp table customer-like with NULL keys plus NOT EXISTS over a table with NULL fk values; compare against SET disabled_optimizers='deliminator'. (2) q22 results unchanged. (3) A NOT EXISTS with an extra non-equality correlated predicate (q21 shape) must keep the old plan. Use the JSON profile trick to confirm the INNER HJ and DELIM_JOIN are gone from q22 and that the orders scan still has the BF.
expected_gain: q22 -12..-20% (about 0.18s of 0.8s CPU removed). Geomean about -1%. Possibly hidden NOT EXISTS templates (q21-like ones stay unchanged because of the equality-only guard).
generality: Any correlated NOT EXISTS with a simple equality correlation and a filtered outer query (anti-joins against fact tables are very common). Could be slower when the outer selection is very selective and the BF auto-disables. In that case the old delim join reduced the RHS before an expensive RHS subtree. SubqueryIsSimple limits the RHS to scans/filters/projections/inner joins, so the extra cost is bounded.
risk: Medium-low. One-line gate change on a path already proven for SEMI in E0021. Main risk is NULL-key semantics for ANTI after the NDF->= conversion; the plan includes explicit tests.

title: Parallel perfect-HJ build + dense INNER builds up to 4M range
hypothesis: The perfect HJ build runs serially inside PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize (physical_hash_join.cpp:1202-1207 -> PerfectHashJoinExecutor::BuildPerfectHashTable -> FullScanHashTable: ScanKeyColumn over all rows, then one data_collection.Gather per payload column, all on one thread). The regular HJ finalize is parallel (ScheduleFinalize). Measured A/B, warm, 8 threads, on near-identical data: lineitem JOIN part with p_partkey<=1048000 (range under MAX_BUILD_SIZE, so perfect HJ) took 153-175ms. The same query with p_partkey<=1049000 (just over the limit, so regular HJ + BF) took 102-125ms, 4 alternating pairs. In JSON profiles the perfect variant has LOWER join CPU (0.20s vs 0.39s) but 57ms HIGHER latency (0.180 vs 0.123s). The serial build is pure wall-clock loss. So today the perfect HJ makes every 0.5M-1M-row dense build slower. That is also why CanDoPerfectHashJoin cannot be opened further: INNER joins with range >1M are rejected even when dense (line 120-121, `!PropagatesBuildSide(op.join_type) ||`). q14 builds part (2M dense keys p_partkey 1..2M, payload p_type VARCHAR) with a regular HJ: HASH_JOIN 0.58s operator time / 1.08s CPU vs a 773k-row probe. This is the biggest operator in q14 (171ms).
plan: Step 1, parallel build: in PerfectHashJoinExecutor (perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp) keep the serial ScanKeyColumn + TemplatedFillSelectionVectorBuild (duplicate check, cheap int work). Time it first with a local timer to confirm the gather dominates. Then build a slot->tuple mapping and split the payload Gather (FullScanHashTable lines 190-199) into tasks over contiguous SLOT ranges aligned to 64. Validity words are written non-atomically by Gather, so tasks must never share a validity word. Schedule them from PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize the same way ScheduleFinalize / HashJoinFinalizeEvent (physical_hash_join.cpp ~line 528) schedules HashJoinFinalizeTask: e.g. a PerfectHashJoinFinalizeEvent whose tasks each call executor.GatherRange(begin,end). Keep the serial path when the build has fewer than ~64k rows. The duplicate/fallback decision stays serial and before scheduling, so the fallback to ScheduleFinalize is unchanged. Do the col_mask.Combine(bitmap_build_idx) per range as well (or keep it serial: it is word-wise and cheap). Step 2: in CanDoPerfectHashJoin, drop the `!PropagatesBuildSide(op.join_type) ||` term, so INNER joins also qualify for range <= MAX_DENSE_BUILD_SIZE (4M) when ht.Count()*2 >= range+1. Validate: rerun the p_partkey<=1048000 vs <=1049000 A/B (the perfect variant should now be at least as fast), then q14 and q13 (RIGHT perfect HJ on 1.5M customer) in the bench. Correctness: compare against SET disabled_optimizers / a variant with a hash-forcing extra condition, including NULL payloads and VARCHAR payloads, INNER and RIGHT.
expected_gain: q14 -15..-25% (2M dense part build becomes a parallel perfect HJ; join CPU roughly halves per the A/B). q13 a few % if its RIGHT perfect build is latency-bound. Any template with a 0.3-1M-row dense build (perfect today) gains up to ~50ms of latency. Geomean -1.5..-3%.
generality: Every FK join against a dense-key dimension (part, customer, supplier, date dims, surrogate keys) at larger scale factors. It removes a serial phase that grows linearly with build size. Could get slower: dense builds whose probe side is tiny. A 4M-slot perfect table is allocated and gathered where the regular HJ would also build 4M entries, so the memory is similar. Sparse perfect HJ stays excluded by the 50% density gate (a prior 8M sparse attempt regressed).
risk: Medium. Concurrent Gather into shared dictionary vectors must not race on validity words or string data, so use slot-range partitioning. Event scheduling in Finalize must keep the perfect/regular fallback logic intact. If the payload gather is not the dominant serial cost, step 1 gains little; the implementer should time it first.

title: Exact BF bitmap up to 2^27 bits when 1024 bits/key allows
hypothesis: In q05 the lineitem scan is the hottest operator: 0.92s CPU out of about 1.7s total, 60M rows in and 2.03M out. Its join filter is a HASHED BF over 455k o_orderkey values spread across a 60M range. TrySetExactBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:1011) caps the exact bitmap at count*128 = 58.3M bits, so this range (59.99M) misses the cap by 3%. I ran a measured A/B with no code change: I widened the orders date window by about 2 weeks, giving ~500k keys, which is enough to cross the cap. The lineitem scan dropped 0.92s -> 0.48s CPU (-48%) even though more rows qualify, and false positives went away (1.99M -> exact 1.88M rows, where the hashed BF let ~10% extra rows through). q05-shaped wall time fell from 331/256/266ms to 244/229/208/230ms (~-15%). An exact bitmap probe costs one bit test with no hashing. The probe keys (lineitem l_orderkey) come in clustered order, so even a multi-MB bitmap stays cache-friendly. Note: an earlier memory entry said raising this cap was low value because it removed only ~10% of rows. That looked at rows only; the CPU saving comes from the cheaper probe.
plan: In src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp, TrySetExactBloomFilter (lines ~1009-1016): keep the 128 bits/key rule and the EXACT_BF_SMALL_RANGE floor, and add a mid tier. The exact bitmap is also allowed if range < MinValue(EXACT_BF_MID_RANGE = 1<<27 bits (16MB), ht.Count() * 1024). In code: key_cap = MaxValue(key_cap, MinValue<idx_t>(EXACT_BF_MID_RANGE, ht.Count()*1024)). Keep the EXACT_BF_MAX_RANGE guard and update the comment that says memory is bounded by the pointer table. Check that the bitmap allocation and zeroing in SetExactRange (bloom filter class) works for 16MB, that the build-side insert for exact mode is thread-safe for the larger size (it is already used up to 2^32 ranges with dense keys), and that the E0021 offset path calls the same function. Validate with the q05 A/B above: o_orderdate < '1995-12-25' (hashed today) must become exact, and the lineitem scan CPU should drop to about 0.48s. Results must match the old build.
expected_gain: q05 -10..-15% (scan CPU -48%). Possibly q03/q07/q08/q21/q18, where sparse orderkey/custkey/partkey BFs sit between 128 and 1024 bits/key over ranges up to 134M. Geomean maybe -1..-2%.
generality: Any FK join where a filtered dimension or fact (orders by date, customers by segment) builds a BF on a key range of up to ~134M values at 0.1-1% density. This is very common for star/snowflake date-filtered joins. Queries that could get slower are those with random (unclustered) probe keys against a 4-16MB bitmap: L3 misses there instead of an L2-resident hashed BF. The 1024 bits/key bound limits that to at most 128 bytes of bitmap per build key. There is also a one-time zeroing cost of up to 16MB per join.
risk: Low. This only changes a threshold on an existing, verified mechanism. The main risks are random-probe cache behaviour and memory per concurrent join.

title: Bundle: fused integer hashed-BF probe + exact BF up to 2^27 bits at 1024 bits/key
hypothesis: In r9, A/B on q05 showed the hashed BF probe costs about 2x the exact-bitmap probe: lineitem scan 0.92s vs 0.48s CPU, wall -15%. The false-positive rows hardly mattered. The extra cost is the probe pipeline in BFTableFilter::Filter (src/planner/filter/bloom_filter.cpp:171). HashInternal slices the key vector into a dictionary vector, VectorOperations::Hash writes a hashes vector, Flatten runs, LookupHashes makes a second pass, and a third pass translates the selection. For integer keys a single fused loop can do all of it: read data[sel[i]], call duckdb::Hash<T>(v) (MurmurHash64, the same hash the build side uses), and do the bf word load and mask test. Part 2 re-lands E0025 unchanged (TrySetExactBloomFilter in physical_hash_join.cpp, middle tier range < min(2^27, count*1024)). It gave q05 -9/-18/-20% with no regressions, but missed the -20.3% bar by itself. The fused probe speeds up every BF that stays hashed: ranges above the caps, more than 1024 bits/key, and hidden templates. The exact tier covers q05.
plan: 1) bloom_filter.cpp, BFTableFilter::Filter, non-exact branch: if keys_v is a FLAT_VECTOR (or DICTIONARY, via ToUnifiedFormat) of an integer physical type (INT8..INT64, UINT8..UINT64), use a new template TemplatedLookupHashed<T>. Model its loop on TemplatedLookupExact (row_sel handling, validity), but compute filter.LookupOne(Hash(static_cast<T>(data[idx]))). The hash must match what VectorOperations::Hash produces for that type. Check this in src/common/vector_operations/vector_hash.cpp: for each T, HashOp uses duckdb::Hash<T>. NULLs: copy the exact path's handling, so an invalid row is not found only when the old path would also have dropped it. The old path hashes NULL to a constant hash, so either keep that behaviour or treat NULL as found (the join filters it anyway). Decide by reading HashOp's null handling. Every other type keeps the existing HashInternal path. 2) physical_hash_join.cpp TrySetExactBloomFilter: re-apply E0025. Add a tier where range < min(1<<27, count*1024), and only multiply when count <= 2^17. Correctness: use temp tables with BIGINT and INTEGER keys plus NULLs, and a build range larger than 2^27 so the filter stays hashed. Compare results against SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown'. Use the warm JSON profile trick to check q05 lineitem scan CPU.
expected_gain: q05 -15..-20%, carried over from E0025. Any template whose BF stays hashed (sparse integer keys over a wide range) gets a 20-40% cheaper BF probe, probably q07/q08/q18/q21-like hidden joins. Visible geomean -1.5..-2.5%.
generality: All runtime join BFs on integer keys, the most common join key type. The fused loop does the same work in fewer passes, so I expect no slowdowns. The 2^27 tier allocates up to 16MB per filter, only for builds of at most 128k keys at 1024 bits/key. Probes with poor locality over 16MB could miss L2 more often, but E0025 showed no regressions.
risk: Low-medium. The probe hash must match the build hash bit for bit, or rows are dropped. That would show up as wrong results, which the correctness checks above catch. Read vector_hash.cpp for each type before relying on Hash<T>.

title: Bundle: per-value BitPacking select for sparse filtered scans + exact BF up to 2^27 bits at 1024 bits/key
hypothesis: (1) In filtered table scans, the non-filter columns are fully decoded even when few rows pass. BitPacking has no `select` callback, so StandardColumnData::Select (standard_column_data.cpp:103) falls back to ColumnData::Select: Scan the whole vector, then result.Slice. Measured hot on lineitem, where every column involved is BitPacking (pragma_storage_info): `max()` over 5 extra columns WHERE l_partkey<100000 (5% pass) takes 88-95ms, and WHERE l_partkey<10000 (0.5% pass) takes 94-95ms. The same filter with count(*) takes 26-28ms. So the ~65ms spent fetching the extra columns does not depend on selectivity at all. A prior-run attempt (auto-memory bitpacking-select-no-gain) decoded only the selected 32-value blocks. At 5% selectivity about 80% of blocks still hold a selected row (1-0.95^32), so it saved almost nothing and got 0%. That was a bad implementation of a good idea. Reading each selected value straight from the bitstream makes the cost scale with sel_count. q09's lineitem scan (60M rows -> 3.27M, 5 extra columns l_suppkey/l_orderkey/l_extendedprice/l_discount/l_quantity) and q05's lineitem scan (60M -> 2.03M, 3 extra columns) are exactly this case. (2) Re-land the E0025 tier, retired twice as a near-miss: q05 -9/-18/-20% and -13.5/-17.9/-17.4% against a -20.3% bar, with no regressions. Adding (1) on q05's own lineitem scan should push q05 past the bar.
plan: Part 1, src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp: add `template <class T> void BitpackingSelect(ColumnSegment &segment, ColumnScanState &state, idx_t vector_count, Vector &result, const SelectionVector &sel, idx_t sel_count)` and register it in GetBitpackingFunction (line ~964) through the CompressionFunction constructor's select slot. Count the nullptr args against rle.cpp:592 / numeric_constant.cpp:221, which pass the select function in that position. Select contract: the result is FLAT and holds the sel_count selected values compacted (result_data[i] = value at sel.get_index(i)), and the scan state advances by vector_count. sel is ascending, as RLESelect assumes. Implementation: use BitpackingScanState (line 608) and walk metadata groups exactly as BitpackingScanPartial (line 775) does. When current_group_offset reaches BITPACKING_METADATA_GROUP_SIZE, call LoadNextGroup. Handle each mode within one metadata group as follows. CONSTANT: write the constant. CONSTANT_DELTA: frame_of_reference + delta*offset, copied from ScanPartial. FOR: per-value extraction, for T of 4 or 8 bytes only. The fastpforlib layout (third_party/fastpforlib/bitpacking.cpp Unroller, 32-bit words, LSB-first) makes each 32-value algorithm group a little-endian bitstream: value j sits at bit j*width from the block start, block start = current_group_ptr + (offset - offset%32)*width/8. Read ceil((bitoff%8 + width)/8) bytes with memcpy so nothing is read past the end, shift, mask, then add current_frame_of_reference with the same unsigned wrapping as the scan path. If width > 56 or T is 1/2/16 bytes, use the existing block unpack instead. DELTA_FOR (needs a prefix sum), or sel_count > vector_count/4: decode with the existing ScanPartial logic into a thread-local scratch buffer, then gather. Finally advance the state by the rows consumed, using the same bookkeeping as Skip/ScanPartial. Verify validity: for NOT NULL columns the validity is Constant, which already has select (numeric_constant.cpp ConstantSelect); ValiditySelect covers the uncompressed case. Correctness: in a debug or temporary check, compare against a full scan. Test via `dbe-tool sql` with TEMP tables of INT/BIGINT/DECIMAL columns containing NULLs, sorted data (DELTA_FOR), constant runs, widths 1..63, and selective filters at 0.1%, 5%, 30% and 90%. Compare with `SET disabled_optimizers` / filters written as `col+0` so the filter is not pushed. Part 2, src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp TrySetExactBloomFilter: add the exact-bitmap tier range < min(2^27, count*1024). Cap the multiplication at 2^27 for EVERY build size, not only count <= 2^17 (E0026 lesson). Keep the 128 bits/key rule, the 2^22 floor and the 2^32 guard. Measure with the warm JSON profile: lineitem scan CPU in q05 and q09 before/after.
expected_gain: Micro: 5-col selective lineitem fetch 95ms -> ~40ms. q09 -5..-8% (5 extra cols at 5.4% pass), q05 -20..-25% (E0025 -17% plus select), q17/q19/q14 a few % (selective lineitem scans via BF or date filters). Geomean about -3..-4%.
generality: Every filtered scan over BitPacking (the default integer/decimal compression) where the filters or join BFs pass under ~25% of rows: TPC-H q06/q12/q14/q15/q17/q19/q20-style scans, star-schema fact scans with BF. Dense filters (>25% pass) keep the current decode path through the threshold, so they should not slow down. DELTA_FOR columns (sorted keys) get no benefit. Part 2 only changes the BF representation for builds with range < 2^27.
risk: Medium. Bit-level extraction must exactly match fastunpack layout and FOR wrap arithmetic; mitigated by restricting to 4/8-byte T with width<=56 and falling back otherwise, plus a randomized sql comparison. The scan state must advance correctly across metadata-group boundaries (mirror ScanPartial). Part 2 has passed hidden validation twice.

title: Exact BF for sparse perfect hash joins, filled from the perfect-HT slot bitmap
hypothesis: In q07 (187ms, 6.2% of total) the lineitem scan emits 18.23M rows, and its only dynamic filter is `optional: l_suppkey>=3 AND <=99999`. The l_suppkey=s_suppkey HASH_JOIN then drops them to 1.46M (8%), costing 0.19s CPU plus a 0.025s projection (warm JSON profile, .dbe/scratch_q07.json). The build has 8016 supplier keys in a 100k range, so it takes the perfect HJ path (range <= MAX_BUILD_SIZE 1M). JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:946) returns false for every perfect hashtable, on the reasoning that 'with a perfect hashtable we expect good min/max pruning'. That only holds for dense builds. Region- or nation-filtered dimension tables (supplier, customer, part under 1M range) are sparse, so min/max prunes nothing. A prior run tried a BF on sparse perfect HJ (q21) and found that rows dropped 37.9M->2.7M but scan CPU rose. That was before two things landed: the exact bitmap BF for small ranges (E0022), whose probe costs about half a hashed one, and the per-value BitPacking select (E0027), which makes the non-filter columns (here l_orderkey, l_extendedprice, l_discount) cost proportional to selectivity. Until E0027 they were fully decoded and then sliced. The perfect HT already holds an exact bitmap of the build keys, bitmap_build_idx (slot = key - build_min), so filling the BF costs a word copy instead of a pass over the HT.
plan: 1) In JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp ~938), stop rejecting a perfect hashtable outright. Allow it when it is sparse: ht->Count() * 4 <= range + 1. Add a parameter, or let the caller compute it, using perfect_join_statistics.build_range or max-min. 2) In FinalizeFilters (~1163), for the perfect case on the no-cast, no-offset path: call TrySetExactBloomFilter(*ht, op, min_val, max_val). The range is < 1M, so the small-range floor always makes it exact. Then add the entry to deferred_bloom_filters as today, but do NOT call ht->SetBuildBloomFilter for the HT finalize, which never runs for a perfect HJ. If the BF did not become exact, skip it. 3) Add PerfectHashJoinExecutor::FillExactBloomFilter(BloomFilter &bf) in perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp/.hpp. It calls bf.Initialize(context, count). It needs exact_min == build_min widened the same way TrySetExactBloomFilter widens it (int64 for signed types) and exact_range == build_range; assert both. It then copies the bitmap_build_idx words into the bf words. Both use 64-bit LSB-first words with bit i == slot i, so bloom_filter.hpp needs an accessor or a friend for the raw word pointer. If bitmap_build_idx.AllValid() (no data pointer), set all bits, or just skip the BF because that case is dense. 4) Push the deferred BFs right after the perfect build is final, through PushBloomFilter. This happens in two places. The serial path is PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize after FinalizeFilters (~1299), when use_perfect_hash is true. The parallel path is PerfectHashJoinBuildEvent::FinishEvent (~656), after FinishBuild returns true. If use_perfect_hash turns out false (duplicates), keep today's behaviour: the regular HT finalize builds and pushes the BF. Make sure the deferred list is not pushed twice and that the BF is not left half-initialized for the fallback. 5) Verify. Check that the q07 lineitem scan shows `l_suppkey IN BF(s_suppkey)` and that its output cardinality drops from 18.2M to ~1.5M, and that results match. Run a micro A/B on q07 hot (3x each). Also check a RIGHT perfect join (q13 customer, dense) and confirm it still gets no BF, because of the density gate.
expected_gain: q07 -8..-15%: about 0.2s CPU of ~1.5s saved in HJ probe and projection, offset by an exact BF probe on 18M rows. Possibly also q02 (ps_suppkey = region-filtered supplier) and q08 (supplier/customer sides). Hidden templates with nation- or region-filtered supplier/customer builds probing lineitem/orders/partsupp (q20, q21-like) should gain too.
generality: Any equi-join whose build is a selective dimension subset with a key range under 1M (perfect HJ), probing a large fact table. This is very common: star joins with region/nation/category filters. Queries where the BF is unselective are protected by the 25% density gate and SelectivityOptionalFilter's runtime auto-disable. Possible slowdown: a probe scan whose BF check costs more than the perfect-HT probe it replaces, which can happen when there are few extra columns and selectivity is moderate (~20%).
risk: Low-medium. The bitmap copy must use exactly the same min and widening as the BF lookup; a mismatch gives wrong results, so test with negative or offset key ranges (e.g. a join on s_suppkey - 50000) and compare against `+0` variants. The fallback-to-regular-HJ path (duplicates) must not push a BF that was never filled.

title: Bundle: sparse perfect-HJ exact BF (E0028) + branch-free fixed 8-byte BitPacking per-value extract
hypothesis: E0028 was a near-miss with no regressions. It got q07 -9.0% in the official run (-11.5/-12.9/-17.7% in the implementer's runs; it needed -13.1%), q02 -7..-22%, visible geomean -1.9% (-3.2% implementer), and hidden validation passed. Today's q07 profile shows why it helps: the lineitem scan feeds the l_suppkey=s_suppkey perfect HJ (0.24s CPU) with 18.2M rows that pass only min/max, and the HJ cuts them to 1.46M. With the slot-bitmap exact BF the scan emits about 1.46M rows. At that density (~8% < 1/4) the other lineitem columns (l_orderkey, l_extendedprice, l_discount, l_shipdate) go through the E0027 per-value BitPacking select. So in q07 the select path now carries most of the decode work, and the same is true for every BF-filtered scan (q05/q08/q09/q14/q19). The per-value extraction, BitpackingExtractValue (bitpacking.cpp:876), does memcpy(&bits, ptr, byte_count) with byte_count computed at runtime. That is a variable-length copy, usually an out-of-line memcpy call plus branches, done for every selected value. r11 measured ~26ns/value over count(*) at 5% pass, which is far above the ~1-2ns a shift-and-mask should cost. Loading a fixed 8 bytes (memcpy with a constant size of 8 compiles to one mov) removes the call. This is Part 2. It speeds up the path E0028 sends more rows into, and it gives a general gain on every sparse-select scan.
plan: Part 1: re-apply E0028 exactly as described in the ledger, keeping all three of its pieces. (a) In physical_hash_join.cpp, JoinFilterPushdownInfo::FinalizeFilters / CanUseBloomFilter (~946): let a perfect HT through when count*4 <= range+1, accept the exact BF only (TrySetExactBloomFilter must succeed), and do not set SetBuildBloomFilter. (b) Add PerfectHashJoinExecutor::FillExactBloomFilter in perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp: InsertExact(build_min widened to 64 bits + slot) for each set bit of bitmap_build_idx, or for every slot if the build is dense. (c) Add a helper PushPerfectHashJoinBloomFilters, called after FinalizeFilters when use_perfect_hash is set, in both the serial PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize path (~1282-1300) and the parallel PerfectHashJoinBuildEvent::FinishEvent (~648, after FinishBuild). Part 2: in src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp, BitpackingSelect FOR branch (~930-940): when the 8-byte read stays inside the segment buffer, load uint64 with memcpy(&bits, p, 8), then shift and mask. Compute a per-call safe limit from the segment handle pointer + segment.SegmentSize() (or the block size), and fall back to the existing variable-length BitpackingExtractValue only for values whose byte offset + 8 exceeds it. Hoist the mask ((1<<width)-1) and the width out of the loop. Optionally also hoist the per-value `group_pos - idx_in_block` arithmetic: block_start = group_ptr + (group_pos/32)*4*width bytes. Test correctness on an ATTACHed file db with force_compression='bitpacking' + CHECKPOINT (TEMP tables are never compressed): compare sum() of a selectively filtered BIGINT/INTEGER column at widths 1..56 against the uncompressed table. Then run the E0028 correctness queries again (negative shifted keys, RIGHT join with a NULL build row, USMALLINT key, parallel sparse build).
expected_gain: q07 -12..-18%, q02 -7..-20% (from E0028). Part 2 adds a few % on the sparse-select scans in q07/q05/q08/q09/q14/q19. Visible geomean -3..-5%.
generality: Part 1: any FK join against a selectively filtered dimension whose key range is <=1M (or <=4M dense) and that the perfect HJ handles: the classic star-schema case. Part 2: every scan whose non-filter BitPacking columns are decoded through a sparse selection (all BF/zone-filtered scans). Possible slowdown: sparse perfect builds whose BF does not filter, but SelectivityOptionalFilter switches those off. Part 2 has no algorithmic change.
risk: Low-medium. Part 1 already passed hidden validation once. In Part 2 an out-of-bounds read at the segment end is the only hazard, and the bounds guard handles it. A wrong shift or mask would show up in the width-sweep test.

title: Large radix aggregate slows 17-35% when more base-table blocks are resident
hypothesis: Reproduced in ONE process (not a bench artifact): q18 is 505-550ms; after q09 (or after just `SELECT sum(l_extendedprice+l_discount+l_partkey+l_suppkey) FROM lineitem; SELECT sum(ps_supplycost) FROM partsupp; SELECT max(p_name) FROM part`) it becomes 630-720ms and stays slow on every later run. The isolated 15M-group agg `SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT l_orderkey FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>312)` goes 458/465ms -> 554-654ms. duckdb_memory() BASE_TABLE goes 369MB -> 881-1067MB. A 15M-row probe HJ (orders x lineitem, l_quantity>49) is unaffected (~110ms). SET allocator_flush_threshold / allocator_bulk_deallocation_flush_threshold = 64GB does NOT fix it. memory_limit is 12.2GB, so this is not eviction pressure. TemporaryMemoryManager::UpdateState (temporary_memory_manager.cpp:121-160) does not read used base-table memory, so the reservation is probably not the cause (to verify). This likely explains why E0009/E0013 (q13 large perfect HA) were retired for q18 +8-10%. In the official bench every template runs with lots of columns resident, so q18's 545ms and q13's 2.09s agg likely include this penalty.
plan:
1) Localize: in one dbe-tool sql call run the agg reproducer 3x, load the extra columns, run 3x again, with EXPLAIN ANALYZE / json profiling before and after. Compare TABLE_SCAN CPU vs HASH_GROUP_BY CPU, and if possible sink vs finalize. Use the InternalException-gated-on-setting trick to dump GetThreadLimit() (radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:163), the reservation, the radix bits and whether the agg went external/abandoned (lines 484-519) in both states.
2) Hypotheses, in order:
(a) Sink thread limit or radix bits differ (reservation or ComputeReservation depends on state) -> fix the computation.
(b) BlockAllocator pool (block_allocator.cpp): base-table loads take the 'touched' blocks the agg freed, so the agg's TupleDataCollection blocks land in other pool regions with worse TLB/THP backing. Try madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) on the pool mmap in AllocateVirtualMemory (:33, Linux only) and check that OnDeallocation's MADV_DONTNEED isn't splitting huge pages on frequently reused blocks.
(c) Eviction-queue / pin-unpin cost grows with the number of resident blocks (buffer_pool.cpp AddToEvictionQueue/PurgeQueue).
3) Land only a mechanism that removes the gap in the reproducer and that does not change behavior under memory pressure.
expected_gain: q18 -10..-15% (its agg dominates). Possibly q13 (2.09s agg CPU) and q16 a few %. Visible geomean -1..-2% if found.
generality: Any large hash aggregation on a warm database with many cached columns, which is the normal hot-run state. If the fix is an allocator/THP change, it affects all buffer-managed memory; queries with small memory footprints should be neutral.
risk: Medium-high on discovery: the cause may be OS-level and unfixable, and the round may yield nothing. Implementation risk is low once localized. A THP madvise could raise RSS.

title: Large perfect HA v3 after the resident-memory agg fix
hypothesis: E0009/E0013 gave q13 -17..-23% in 10/10 runs but were retired for q18 +8.7%. The in-process reproducer shows q18's agg slows whenever memory state changes (more resident blocks), so that regression was the same phenomenon as the resident-memory issue, not a cost of the perfect HA. Once that issue lands, re-landing E0013 should clear q13's 14% threshold without the q18 hit.

Before benchmarking, check in-process that q18 after q13 is unchanged.

title: Faster substring search: rare-pair candidate test + exact multi-literal LIKE in prefilter
hypothesis: Orders scan, sum(o_custkey): with NOT LIKE '%special%packages%' 148-166ms; with '%packages%' alone ~155-160ms; with '%zzzqx%' ~110ms; length() only ~95ms. So the cost of finding 'packages' (2.25M/15M rows hit) is ~50ms of wall over decode. risk: Low; correctness depends on exact boundary handling.

title: Bundle: fallback block reuse cache + large perfect HA v3
hypothesis: Two mechanisms that were each retired on acceptance alone, not on correctness. (1) The r14 fallback block cache: a bounded 64MB queue of freed 256KB blocks in BlockAllocator when block_allocator_memory=0. It fixed the warm-state slowdown of the big radix agg in-process (agg 550-714 -> 460-475ms, q18 warm 630-720 -> 500-518ms). In the bench, join templates gained (q04 -5..-12%, q07 -9% in 2 of 3 runs, q03 -12%, q05 -6..-9%), but no single template cleared its noise threshold. (2) E0013 large perfect HA (22 bits, striped combine, parallel source, lazy init, DELIM guard, buffer-allocator tables) gave q13 -17..-23% in 10 of 10 runs, clearing q13's 14% threshold. Large perfect HA helps GROUP BY on dense integer FK keys up to a 4M range with many rows per group. Risk of slowdown: sparse inputs with overestimated cardinality, measured +60% on a 1.8M-row/2M-slot case. The cache holds up to 64MB more memory.
