title: Clustered-key radix agg: skip finalize combine for interval-disjoint groups
hypothesis: q18 (527ms, 19% of total, the largest template) is ~90% the IN-subquery `SELECT l_orderkey FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>312`. Measured alone it runs ~498ms hot, and its scan alone is 19ms. So the 15M-group radix aggregate costs ~480ms (~256ns per group). An earlier ablation of a 15M-group agg found that skipping the finalize Combine entirely saves 24% (455->345ms): append+InitializeStates is 15% and probe is 10%. In a clustered input nearly every group has exactly one partial state, so that combine work is wasted. Speeding up the sink probe was tried before (run-collapse, in-place finalize) and did not help. lineitem is physically clustered on l_orderkey, as are most fact tables loaded in key or time order. Each sink chunk is then sorted on the first group key, and different chunks overlap only at their endpoint keys. If we can prove that the main HT's partial groups are duplicate-free across threads and abandon generations, each partition can go straight to READY_TO_SCAN, as the existing single_ht path already does.
plan:
All changes in src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp, plus the RadixHTLocalSinkState and RadixHTGlobalSinkState fields in the same file or its header.
(1) Gate the path on: the first group column is an integral physical type; no grouping sets or grouping functions; no DISTINCT aggregates; number_of_threads > GROW_STRATEGY_THREAD_THRESHOLD (abandon mode); not external.
(2) In RadixPartitionedHashTable::Sink, after PopulateGroupChunk, check with one pass over the first key column (no NULLs) that the chunk is non-decreasing. If it is, split the rows with SelectionVectors: rows whose key equals the chunk min or chunk max (the first and last runs) go to a second, small per-thread 'boundary' GroupedAggregateHashTable created via CreateHT. Interior rows go to the main HT with the same filter, through sliced group_chunk/payload_input. For the chunk, record the open interval (min,max), merging it with the previous interval when contiguous, and record its min and max in a boundary-key list. If any chunk is unsorted or has NULL keys, or the interval list passes a cap (e.g. 64k), mark the thread 'unclustered' and send all rows to the main HT from then on.
(3) In Combine, move the intervals, the boundary-key list and the boundary HT's partitioned data into the global state under the lock. Keep boundary data separate from uncombined_data, and store its allocator.
(4) In Finalize, if no thread is unclustered: sort all intervals and check that a.max <= b.min for neighbours (interior keys are strictly inside), then binary-search each boundary key against the intervals. If both checks pass, mark every main partition READY_TO_SCAN and finalize_done++ (copy the single_ht branch). Append the boundary data as extra AggregatePartitions that take the normal FINALIZE/combine task path. If either check fails, Combine the boundary partitioned data into uncombined_data (same radix bits; repartition if needed, using GrowAbandonedDataToRadixBits-like logic) and take the normal path.
(5) Keep count_before_combining and the temporary memory reservation consistent.
Testing: GROUP BY on a clustered key (lineitem l_orderkey, sum/count/min/avg/HAVING) must match the results with the feature disabled. Also test a shuffled-order table (ORDER BY random() into a temp table), which must fall back, and a table with duplicate keys spread across distant row groups (UNION ALL of the same table), where the interval check must fail.
expected_gain: q18 -15..-25% (agg ~480ms; skipping combine saved 24% in ablation, minus the split cost). Geomean about -1.5..-2%. q03 might also gain a little (GROUP BY l_orderkey,... over a lineitem probe that stays clustered).
generality: Any high-cardinality GROUP BY whose leading key is clustered in the input: tables loaded in key or time order (order ids, event ids, timestamps), and join outputs that keep probe order. Unclustered inputs pay one sortedness pass over the first chunk, then disable themselves, which costs ~0. The worst case is data that stays sorted per chunk but overlaps across threads: the interval check fails after paying for the split and the boundary HT, which should be small overhead.
risk: Medium-high. This is correctness-critical: a wrong disjointness proof gives duplicate groups. That is mitigated by strict open-interval checks plus boundary-key checks, and by falling back to the normal combine on any doubt. There is more code than usual in the sink and finalize. The boundary HT also needs its allocator to be stored, otherwise aggregate states dangle.

title: Partition-staged sink for large perfect hash aggregate
hypothesis:
The large perfect hash aggregate (is_large, 13-22 bits) is limited by cache misses. Each thread keeps a private table: q13's c_custkey has 2M slots × 8B, plus a 2MB is_set array, about 18MB per thread and about 144MB for 8 threads. Every input row then does a random read-modify-write that misses L2/L3. Evidence: q13 PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY takes 0.85s CPU (about 28% of the 377ms wall time). A micro test, `SELECT o_custkey, count(o_orderkey) FROM orders GROUP BY o_custkey` (15M rows, 1M groups), shows the cost per row:
- At 8 threads it runs 117ms wall with HA CPU 0.94s, about 62ns/row. The plain scan is 9ms.
- On 1 thread it takes 241-337ms. The same query grouped by o_orderdate (a 2.4K-slot table) takes 92ms on 1 thread.
- Time is roughly linear in input rows (1.87M rows: 30ms; 3.75M: 55ms; 15M: 117ms), so fixed costs such as allocation, page faults and combine are small (about 15ms).

Staging rows by slot stripe before updating should fix this. Each flush then touches only one stripe of about 512KB, which stays in L2, so most misses become L2 hits. The staging writes are sequential per stripe.
plan:
Code: src/execution/perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp (AddChunkLazy, around line 213) and its header. physical_perfecthash_aggregate.cpp (Sink around line 138, Combine around line 187) needs only a call to the new flush.

1. Gate. Enable staging only when lazy_init is set, total_groups * (tuple_size + 1) > 2MB, and all payload types are fixed-width (no VARCHAR/LIST). Aggregate filters may be allowed if their boolean filter column is staged like any other payload column; otherwise gate them off.
2. Add a local staging structure to PerfectAggregateHashTable. It has P partitions, one per stripe of LARGE_PERFECT_HT_STRIPE_SIZE (2^16) slots; move that constant into the header or pass it in. Each partition has a DataChunk with STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE capacity, holding the payload types plus one UBIGINT column for the slot index. Allocate partitions lazily on first use.
3. New AddChunkStaged(groups, payload):
   - Compute the slot indices with ComputeGroupLocation and the existing bounds check.
   - Counting-sort row indices into one SelectionVector per stripe (stripe = slot >> 16).
   - For each non-empty stripe, flush first if its chunk would overflow. Then VectorOperations::Copy each payload column with that sel into the partition chunk at offset size (this keeps validity), write the slot indices, and SetCardinality.
4. FlushPartition(p) reuses the AddChunkLazy body, but takes the slot indices from the staged UBIGINT column instead of recomputing them: addresses = data + slot * tuple_size, lazy is_set initialization, then UpdateStates / UpdateFilteredStates on the staged payload chunk. Reset the chunk afterwards.
5. Add FlushAll(). Call it from PhysicalPerfectHashAggregate::Combine before the striped CombineRange; it is done per thread, on the local table.
6. When the gate is false, Sink keeps calling AddChunkLazy unchanged.

Correctness checks: compare against `SET perfect_ht_threshold=8` (radix path) on these queries:
- count/sum/min/max with NULL payloads (the q13 LEFT JOIN count(o_orderkey))
- NULL group keys (slot 0)
- multi-column groups
- FILTER clauses
- avg over DOUBLE, where only last-digit float differences are acceptable

Then time the micro query above on 1 and 8 threads.
expected_gain: q13: if HA CPU drops from 0.85s to about 0.35s, that is about 60ms wall, or -12..-18%. Other visible templates use large perfect HA little, so expect about 0 for them. Visible geomean about -1..-1.5%. The micro query should go from 117ms to about 60ms.
generality:
Any GROUP BY on dense integer keys with 2^18-2^22 distinct groups (customer/part/supplier keys, dates × small dims) whose input is not clustered on the key. These get faster whenever the per-thread table is bigger than L2. Workloads that could get slower:
- Inputs already clustered on the key, where the old path hits cache anyway; staging then adds about 3-5ns/row of copying.
- Very small inputs, which pay for allocating the staging chunks.

The 2MB table-size gate limits both cases. Small perfect HAs are untouched.
risk:
Medium.
- Correctness: validity must be copied through staging. Filters and the payload_idx bookkeeping must match AddChunkLazy. A flush missed before Combine silently loses rows. Each of these is caught by the A/B against perfect_ht_threshold=8.
- Performance: the per-stripe VectorOperations::Copy overhead (32 stripes × columns per chunk) could eat the gain when there are many payload columns. A fallback is to gate on payload column count ≤ 4.

title: Parallel hash-join finalize for medium builds (64K-1M rows)
hypothesis: PhysicalHashJoin finalizes the hash table on a single thread whenever the build has fewer than PARALLEL_CONSTRUCT_THRESHOLD = 1,048,576 rows (physical_hash_join.cpp:388, FinalizeSingleThreaded:403). That covers both the pointer-table init memset and the Finalize/InsertHashes loop, which also fills the BF. On 8 threads, every 100K-1M row build therefore runs as a serial phase of about 40ns/row before probing can start. I measured this with a 703K-row temp-table build joined against a 15M-row orders probe: the default (serial finalize) took 77-107ms, and with PRAGMA verify_parallelism (forced parallel finalize, despite its 1-chunk-per-task overhead) it took 64-67ms. That is about 25ms of wall time saved on one join. TPC-H-style plans contain many builds of this size: q03 has a 300K customer build (that HJ is 0.20s CPU in the profile), and q05/q07/q08/q09/q02/q22 have filtered dimension and partsupp builds.
plan:
In src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp:
(1) Lower PARALLEL_CONSTRUCT_THRESHOLD from 1048576 to about 65536 rows. Keep the num_threads==1 and KeysAreSkewed checks unchanged.
(2) In HashJoinFinalizeEvent::Schedule, make the chunk count per task adaptive. CHUNKS_PER_TASK=64 means 131K rows per task, so a 300K build would get only 3 tasks. Use chunks_per_task = clamp(chunk_count / (4 * num_threads), 4, 64).
(3) In HashJoinTableInitEvent, check whether MINIMUM_ENTRIES_PER_TASK=131072 still makes sense. It probably does, because the memset is cheap.
Before the bench, A/B on the micro query with the threshold at 1M vs 64K: CREATE TEMP TABLE b AS SELECT o_orderkey bk, o_shippriority bp FROM orders WHERE o_orderkey % 256 < 3; SELECT count(*), sum(bp) FROM b JOIN orders o ON bk=o.o_orderkey. Also try 300K and 100K builds (% 256 < 1, and smaller). Check that results are identical, including with duplicate build keys: build from lineitem l_orderkey, so there are many duplicates per key, which exercises chain insert under CAS.
expected_gain: Roughly 3-15ms of wall time per medium-size HJ build. q03 (customer 300K build) -3..-6%; q05/q07/q08/q09/q02/q22 a few % each; visible geomean maybe -2..-4%.
generality: Every hash join with a 64K-1M row build on a multi-threaded machine, which is the most common join size class in star-schema analytics. Builds under 64K rows are unchanged. Possible slowdown: builds just above 64K that previously ran serial could pay CAS and task-scheduling overhead (~µs per task). Very skewed keys still use the single-thread path.
risk: Low. The parallel InsertHashesLoop<true> path is already used for builds over 1M rows, so this only moves the threshold. Main risk is a small regression from atomic CAS cost on 64K-200K builds; tune the threshold if the micro A/B shows it.

title: Skip unused local table allocation in staged large perfect HA
hypothesis: After E0034, each thread's local PerfectAggregateHashTable still allocates an 18MB table it never writes to, and zeroes a 2MB is_set array, even when the sink flushes straight into the shared global table. That is about 16MB of memset plus allocator churn per q13 run. The implementer flagged it as a follow-up.
plan: In physical_perfecthash_aggregate.cpp, when the shared staged sink is active (SetStageTarget), construct the local table lazily or in a staging-only mode that skips the data and is_set allocation (perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp AddChunkLazy and UpdateLazy). Keep the old path for small tables.
generality: Every large-range perfect HA (GROUP BY dense FK keys).
risk: Low; small gain, possibly inside q13's 14% noise.

title: Streaming run aggregation for interior rows of clustered-key radix agg
hypothesis: q18 (466ms, 18.7% of total) is dominated by the subquery agg `GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>312`: 60M rows into 15M groups, HASH_GROUP_BY 4.12s CPU against a 0.87s scan. Warm micro at 8 threads: scan plus sum(l_quantity) takes 58ms; the GROUP BY with sum takes 415ms; a plain GROUP BY l_orderkey (distinct) takes 271ms; orders GROUP BY o_orderkey takes 238ms. So nearly all the cost is creating and materializing 15M groups in the radix HT (pointer table, TupleData rows, partitioning, finalize) plus the state updates. It is not the probes: an earlier ablation put probes at about 10%, and collapsing runs before the probe gained only 1-3%. E0033 (SinkClustered, radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:655-749) already splits each sorted chunk into boundary runs, which go to boundary_ht, and interior rows whose keys lie strictly inside (min,max). It proves at finalize that interior intervals are disjoint across all chunks (ClusteredIntervalsDisjoint). Each interior run is then a complete group, yet those rows still go through lstate.ht->AddChunk (line 745): full hashing, probing, row materialization and later partition finalize. Aggregating interior runs directly needs no hash table: one state per run, a state-pointer vector with all rows of a run pointing at the same state, and one call to the aggregate's normal `update(inputs, aggr_input_data, input_count, states_vector, count)`. That removes the group-materialization cost for nearly all groups.
plan:
In src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp, in SinkClustered, for the interior slice [first_end, last_start):
1. Compute run starts with a linear scan of the leading key. The key is already sorted, and the other group columns must be equal within the run; to stay simple, require a single group column or check that all group columns are equal on run change.
2. Allocate one aggregate-state block per run from a per-thread ArenaAllocator and initialize the states.
3. Build a Vector of state pointers, one per row pointing at its run's state, and call each aggregate's update (the same call path as RowOperations::UpdateStates / GroupedAggregateHashTable::AddChunk uses after FindOrCreateGroups).
4. Append the run-head group values (Slice the group chunk with a sel of run heads) and a state-pointer column to a per-thread ColumnDataCollection, the 'run store'.
In Finalize/Source:
- If the clustered proof succeeds (the existing ClusteredIntervalsDisjoint path), the source additionally scans each run store: finalize the states chunk by chunk into the aggregate output columns with the same layout and column order the radix source produces for HT partitions, then destroy the states. This must be parallel across run-store chunks or threads.
- If the proof fails, fall back by combining every run-store chunk into the global/partition HT: FindOrCreateGroups on the group chunk, then RowOperations::CombineStates (or the equivalent used by GroupedAggregateHashTable::Combine) from source pointers to target pointers, then run the normal finalize.
Gate it like the existing clustered path, plus: single grouping set, no FILTER, no DISTINCT and no ORDER BY aggregates; destructors are called. Add a session-independent kill switch only if one already exists for E0033. Verify against `SET disabled_optimizers` / threads=1, and against a table whose chunks are internally sorted but globally overlapping (e.g. `SELECT (i%1000000)//4 k` built in reverse blocks), so the fallback runs. Test sum, avg, min, max, count, list and first on 1 and 8 threads, NULL keys, NULL payloads, and empty input.
expected_gain: q18 -20..-35% (subquery agg 415ms → ~150ms in micro terms); possibly q03, whose join output is probed in l_orderkey order and grouped on l_orderkey first. Geomean -2..-3%.
generality: Any GROUP BY whose leading integral key is physically clustered: primary/serial ids, time-ordered fact tables, and aggregates over join output that preserves a sorted probe order. Unclustered input is untouched (the E0033 gate already detects it). Data that is sorted inside each chunk but overlaps globally gets slower through the fallback combine, but that case is already slower under E0033.
risk: Medium-high. A new source path must match the radix HT output layout exactly, and the states need correct lifetime and destruction. The fallback must be correct when the disjointness proof fails. Aggregates with order-sensitive semantics (first, list) stay correct, because runs are processed in row order.

title: Partition-local slot addressing for in-memory HJ finalize
hypothesis: Hash-join builds over 1M rows are expensive per row, even with no probe. q03's o_orderkey HJ costs 0.20s CPU when the probe side is empty: count(*) with l_shipdate > 1998-11-30 gives 0 probe rows, and the build has 1.45M rows, so that is about 137ns per build row. Payload width does not matter: count(*) costs the same as the full q03 payload. In hot q03 the HJ is 0.38s of 1.08s user. In hot q09 the o_orderkey=l_orderkey HJ (3.27M-row build) is 0.80s of 2.65s user, the largest operator. The pointer table is NextPowerOfTwo(count*load_factor) entries, i.e. 4M x 8B = 32MB for q03. InsertHashesLoop (join_hashtable.cpp:591) linear-probes at slot = hash & bitmask, the LOW hash bits. The sink, however, radix-partitions on HIGH bits: RadixPartitioning::Shift/Mask, the bits just below the 16-bit salt. Each finalize task's chunk range therefore scatters inserts over the whole 32MB table, roughly one cache/TLB miss per row. If the slot index is the top log2(capacity) bits below the salt, i.e. slot = (hash >> (48 - log2cap)) & bitmask, the slot's top bits equal the radix partition bits. Every partition then owns a contiguous capacity/2^radix_bits region (2MB for q03), and a finalize task working inside one partition writes L2/L3-resident memory.
plan: 1) First verify cheaply with a temporary timer or a perf breakdown that the finalize insert dominates the build CPU on the q03 build-only micro (shown in memory). If sink append dominates instead, stop and report. 2) In JoinHashTable (src/include/duckdb/execution/join_hashtable.hpp and src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp), add a member `slot_shift`, set in InitializePointerTable/AllocatePointerTable (~line 787-817). For the in-memory single-round path, use 48 - log2(capacity), clamped at >= 0. For the external/partitioned-round path (PrepareExternalFinalize, physical_hash_join.cpp ~1244 sets EXTERNAL_LOAD_FACTOR), keep 0, i.e. today's low bits. A round holds only a subset of partitions, so high-bit slots would cluster there. 3) Apply the shift everywhere a slot is derived: ApplyBitmaskAndGetSaltBuild, the probe-side bitmask application (~line 151-161, GetRowPointers and the salt/offset code), and any other `& bitmask` use (grep it). Linear-probe wrap-around stays `& bitmask`. The salt stays the top 16 bits. 4) Make the finalize tasks (physical_hash_join.cpp, the parallel finalize with chunks_per_task) iterate chunks in partition order. Check that data_collection is combined partition by partition. If it is not, combine it that way, or give each task a single partition's chunk range. 5) Correctness checks: INNER/LEFT/RIGHT/FULL/SEMI/ANTI/MARK joins, NULL keys, a forced external join (small memory_limit), duplicate-heavy keys, and both sides of PARALLEL_CONSTRUCT_THRESHOLD.
expected_gain: Builds over 1M rows. q03 HJ 0.38s→~0.25s (-5..-10%); q09 orderkey HJ 0.80s (-5..-8%); smaller gains on q05/q07/q08/q18/q21-like plans. Estimated geomean -2..-4% if the finalize-insert share is as large as the miss model predicts.
generality: Any in-memory hash join whose pointer table is larger than L2/L3 (>~500K build rows), which covers most fact-to-dimension and fact-to-fact joins. Small builds are unchanged, since their table fits in cache either way. The external path is left as is.
risk: Medium-high. Slot addressing must be identical on build and probe, or rows will be missed: test every join type and the external path. A poor hash high-bit distribution could lengthen probe chains, but DuckDB hashes are murmur-mixed. If the finalize share is small, the gain is too, so step 1 gates the work.

title: Huge-page backed hash-join pointer table for large builds
hypothesis: Large in-memory HJ builds cost ~100-200ns per build row, and more than half of that is not the input scan. Build-only micro (hot, 8 threads; lineitem 1995 = 9.1M build rows, 0 probe rows, forced with SET disabled_optimizers='join_order,build_side_probe_side'): HJ query 1.34s user + 0.42s SYS vs 0.40s user / 0 sys for the bare scan. That leaves about 0.95s user, ~104ns per row, plus 0.4s of kernel time. BF fill is only ~0.1s of it (join_filter_pushdown off: 1.21-1.24s). In hot q07 the middle HJ builds 1.46M lineitem rows and probes 100K orders: 0.287s CPU (~196ns per build row). q09's o_orderkey HJ (3.27M build) takes 0.80s and q03's (1.45M build) 0.38s. E0037 showed that partition-local slots do not shrink the working set. The pointer table is NextPowerOfTwo(count*2) 8-byte entries (join_hashtable.hpp:417): 32MB for 1.45M rows and 256MB for 9.1M. It comes from buffer_manager.GetBufferAllocator().Allocate (join_hashtable.cpp:804/812). jemalloc runs with oversize_threshold 256MB, so the biggest tables are fresh mmaps every query, and the faults and zeroing show up as sys time. Each insert in InsertHashes and each probe in GetRowPointers touches a random 8-byte slot. With 4KB pages a 32-256MB table covers 8K-65K pages, far beyond the L2 TLB (~1.5K entries), so nearly every slot access is a TLB miss plus a page walk on top of the cache miss. With 2MB pages the same table is 16-128 pages, so walks mostly disappear and faults drop 512x.
plan: Step 0 (cheap gate): Read /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled and defrag. If enabled is [never], abandon. If [always], the table may already be THP-backed: then check whether the allocation is 2MB-aligned and whether jemalloc's opt_thp or the decay settings defeat it, and measure before coding. Step 1: In src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp JoinHashTable::AllocatePointerTable, when capacity*sizeof(ht_entry_t) >= 4MB (Linux only, #ifdef __linux__), allocate the table so that it is 2MB-aligned and call madvise(ptr, size, MADV_HUGEPAGE) before the first touch. The first touch is InitializePointerTable's std::fill_n, which runs in the parallel finalize tasks. Simplest way: over-allocate by 2MB through the same BufferAllocator (memory accounting unchanged), keep the AllocatedData, and set `entries` to the 2MB-aligned address inside it. Keep hash_map.GetSize() consistent, or keep the usable capacity in a separate member: the reuse branch at :801 divides GetSize() by the entry size and the D_ASSERT at :815 compares sizes, so both need adjusting. Alternatively add a small helper next to the block_allocator.cpp madvise code (src/storage/block_allocator.cpp:72-77) that mmaps 2MB-aligned memory with MADV_HUGEPAGE, freed by munmap through a custom PrivateAllocatorData. Step 2: rerun the build-only micro above, the q07 query and q09, and compare user and sys time with the madvise on and off (a temporary env var or setting is fine during testing; remove it before landing). Optionally apply the same helper to the GroupedAggregateHashTable entries array only if it is the same few lines; otherwise leave it for a follow-up.
expected_gain: HJ build and probe CPU on large builds -20..-40% when TLB misses dominate: q09 (0.80s HJ), q07 (0.29s), q03 (0.38s), q05/q08 (similar lineitem-orders joins), q18 outer joins. Roughly -3..-6% geomean if the TLB hypothesis holds; also removes ~0.4s sys per 9M-row build.
generality: Every hash join with more than ~250K build rows (pointer table >= 4MB) on Linux, which is every big fact-to-fact or fact-to-dimension join. Small joins are unchanged, below the threshold. Possible slowdowns: THP compaction stalls when memory is fragmented (defrag setting), and an extra 2MB of slack per large table.
risk: Low-medium. The change is contained to allocation, with no change to hashing semantics. The risks are pointer-alignment bookkeeping with the reuse path in AllocatePointerTable and environment dependence on the THP mode (step 0 gates it). Gain may be small if the kernel already backs these mappings with THP.

title: Huge pages for large join tables v2: HJ pointer table >=8MB + perfect-HJ slot arrays
hypothesis: E0038 (THP-backed HJ pointer table for tables >=32MB) just missed acceptance. q09 came in at -7.0% against a noise threshold of 8.6%; implementer runs gave q09 -8.4/-15/-9.3%, q03 -3..-13% and q08 -8%, with nothing slower once free-time DONTNEED+NOHUGEPAGE was added. At 32MB the threshold left the second big random-access join in q09 on 4KB pages. That is the (ps_partkey,ps_suppkey) HJ: build 435K rows, 1M slots = 8MB pointer table, probed 3.27M times, 0.49s of q09's 2.65s CPU. An 8MB table is beyond the 4KB-page L2 TLB reach (~6MB), so every probe costs a TLB miss plus a page walk. The same applies to perfect-HJ slot_to_row/build_bits arrays sized to the key range (perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:158/162). q13's RIGHT perfect HJ over 1.5M customers uses a 12MB slot_to_row array, and the sparse perfect HJs in q07/q02 behave the same way. Huge pages for every random-access join table of 8MB or more should push q09 well past its noise and add gains on q03/q08/q13.
plan: 1) Re-apply E0038 in src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp as described in the ledger. Allocate through BufferAllocator with 2MB slack and align `entries` to 2MB. Call madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) before InitializePointerTable, only when /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled is [madvise] or [always]. PointerTableUsableSize() handles non-power-of-two padded sizes. On free, in the destructor, Reset() and the grow path, call MADV_DONTNEED then MADV_NOHUGEPAGE; this step is mandatory, or q02 gets 5-9% slower. 2) Lower the threshold from 32MB to 8MB (1M slots). 3) Factor the align+madvise+cleanup logic into a small static helper or RAII struct in join_hashtable.cpp, or a new common header. Use it in PerfectHashJoinExecutor (src/execution/operator/join/perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:158-162, and slot_found_match at 297/418) when an array is >=8MB, in place of make_unsafe_uniq_array. 4) Measure q09, q16, q03 and q02 alone several times each before the full bench. Watch q16 in particular: its table is 8MB with 296K build rows, and it swung -14..+7% at a 4MB threshold. If q16 is slower beyond its noise, gate on build rows >= 400K instead.
generality: Any hash join whose build exceeds ~250K rows, or any perfect HJ over a key range of 1M or more. That covers FK joins against fact tables and large dimensions. Small joins are untouched. A query with a mid-size build that runs only once may pay THP fault/compaction cost.
risk: Medium-low. Memory is tracked by the same allocator. The main hazard is huge-page state leaking into recycled jemalloc memory, which the free-time cleanup handles. q16 is borderline at the 8MB threshold.

title: Coalesce sparse filtered scan chunks before emitting
hypothesis: After a selective table filter or join BF, the table scan emits one DataChunk per 2048-row storage vector, even when only a few rows pass. Every operator downstream then pays its fixed per-chunk overhead on tiny chunks. Hot evidence: in q08 (127ms, 0.77s CPU), HASH_JOIN l_partkey=p_partkey takes 0.405s CPU (52% of the query) for only 403K probe rows. Those rows arrive as about 29K chunks of about 14 rows each, because the exact BF from part passes 0.67% of lineitem's 60M rows. Isolated micro `SELECT count(*) FROM lineitem, part WHERE p_partkey=l_partkey AND p_type='PROMO BURNISHED TIN'`: HJ 0.112s for 403K sparse probe rows, which is 277ns/row. The same join with join_filter_pushdown disabled and dense input (l_orderkey<1600000, 1.6M probe rows) takes 0.039s, which is 25ns/row. That leaves about 3.5us of fixed cost per chunk (the probe key executor, Probe/ScanStructure init, two ExecuteInternal calls per chunk, CachingOperator, and the sink downstream). If the scan fills output chunks to at least about 1K rows, that per-chunk cost is paid about 70x fewer times. Note: memory.md lists 'compacting sparse scan chunks' as refuted, but there is no ledger record of it. This measurement is new, direct evidence that the cost is per chunk and not per row.
plan: In src/function/table/table_scan.cpp, DuckTableScanState::TableScanFunc (~line 316): after storage.Scan returns a non-empty chunk with output.size() < COALESCE_MIN (e.g. STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/4 = 512), and the scan is not is_create_index, keep calling storage.Scan into a per-local-state scratch DataChunk (TableScanLocalState, initialized with the output types). Stop when the accumulated size reaches the target, or when storage.Scan returns 0 rows (the assigned parallel range is exhausted, so the batch/row-group boundary and batch index are preserved). Append each scratch result into output with DataChunk::Append, which flattens dictionary/FSST/constant vectors. Only the few selected rows get copied, so decoding them is cheap. If a scratch chunk would overflow STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE, keep it as a pending chunk in local state and emit it first on the next call (output.Reference/Move or Append into the empty output). Handle both the CanRemoveFilterColumns path (scan into all_columns, then ReferenceColumns projection_ids; coalesce after projection, or coalesce all_columns before projecting) and the direct path. Only coalesce when the scan has table filters or dynamic filters (input.filters non-empty), so unfiltered scans stay zero-copy. Do not advance NextParallelScan inside the coalesce loop. Verify on q08 that HJ l_partkey time drops in the JSON profile, and check q13 (FSST orders scan with NOT LIKE, about 98% selectivity, so it is never below threshold) for no regression.
expected_gain: q08 -20..-35% (HJ 0.405s of 0.77s CPU). Also selective-BF lineitem scans in q17 (0.1% pass), q05 (3%), q07, q09, q19, q02, q14. Geomean maybe -3..-6%.
generality: Any scan with a selective filter (pushed predicate, zone-map-surviving range, or join BF/min-max) feeding joins, projections or aggregates. This is very common in star-schema queries. Could be slower: scans at 10-25% selectivity, where the copy cost approaches the saved overhead (hence the low threshold), and LIMIT queries that read slightly more vectors before stopping.
risk: Medium. It touches the core scan path. Pending-chunk carry-over and the CanRemoveFilterColumns projection must be correct. Row-id columns and batch indexes must stay within one parallel range. Order is preserved because coalescing is sequential within one thread's range.

title: Raise operator output caching threshold to 256 rows (sparse HJ/FILTER output coalescing)
hypothesis: E0040 showed that downstream operators pay a fixed cost per chunk (about 3.5us per chunk in HJ probe). Merging filtered scan chunks below 256 rows (STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/8) cut the geomean 9.3% with no regressions. The same merging already exists for operator outputs in CachingPhysicalOperator (src/execution/physical_operator.cpp SelectExecutionMode, used by PhysicalJoin, PhysicalFilter and PhysicalCrossProduct). But it only triggers for chunks of at most CACHE_THRESHOLD = 64 rows (physical_operator.hpp:270). Join and filter outputs with 65-255 rows per chunk pass through unmerged, and every operator above them pays the per-chunk cost. Examples: joins against a filtered dimension that keep 6-25% of rows (region, nation or segment joins) and post-join FILTERs. In q07 hot, the n1/n2 OR FILTER keeps 50%, and 1/5 or 2/25 selective dimension joins are common in q02, q03, q05, q07 and q08. Also, every flush calls make_uniq<DataChunk> plus cached_chunk->Initialize, which reallocates the full vector set each time.
plan: 1) In src/include/duckdb/execution/physical_operator.hpp, change CachingPhysicalOperator::CACHE_THRESHOLD from 64 to STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/8 (256 at the default vector size). Keep the existing ORDERED/PARTITIONED/continuation logic in SelectExecutionMode unchanged; it already handles correctness for every threshold. 2) Optional, if cheap: in CachingPhysicalOperator::Execute (physical_operator.cpp ~443-460), avoid the make_uniq<DataChunk> temporary in RETURN_CACHED_APPEND_CHUNK. Do this by keeping a second owned DataChunk in CachingOperatorState and swapping the two, instead of re-Initializing (allocating) after every Move. 3) Measure thresholds 128 and 256 on full bench. Check q22 and q04 alone, because the scan version regressed q22 at 512 rows, where copying about 260 rows/chunk cost as much as it saved. Report which HJ/FILTER operators in q03/q07/q08 change chunk counts (operator timing of the parents).
expected_gain: A few % on join-heavy templates with selective dimension joins (q02, q03, q05, q07, q08); geomean -1..-3%. Uncertain, because scan-level coalescing (E0040) already densified the biggest sources.
generality: Every pipeline where a hash join, filter or cross product drops most but not almost all rows. This is generic across star/snowflake joins. Queries whose operator outputs sit at 150-256 rows/chunk pay a copy that may cost about what it saves (the q22-style break-even), so 128 is the fallback threshold.
risk: Low. The mechanism and its order-preserving modes already exist and are tested; only the threshold changes. Main risk is a small regression from extra copies near break-even.

title: Evaluate LIKE/contains on FSST codes without decoding filter-only columns
hypothesis: q13 (313ms, the slowest template) is dominated by the orders TABLE_SCAN with o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%': 2.17s of operator CPU (profile.md), out of about 2.1s user time for the whole query. Most of that is FSST decode: decoding 15M strings is the cost, and the substring prefilter (column_segment.cpp TrySubstringPrefilter) only runs after the decode. o_comment is stored as plain FSST (pragma_storage_info: 977 FSST segments + 123 Constant), and p_name is FSST too (98 segments). FSST has no `filter` callback (fsst.cpp registers only scan/select/fetch), so StandardColumnData::Filter (standard_column_data.cpp:76) falls back to ColumnData::Filter, which decodes everything and then filters. In q13 o_comment is filter-only: after filtering, TableScan drops it via projection_ids (table_scan.cpp:213/239), so the decoded strings are thrown away. Patterns made only of literals and '%' can be matched exactly by a small DFA (a KMP chain over the literals). Lifting that DFA to FSST symbols (state x code -> state, one table per segment symbol table) evaluates the predicate in one table lookup per code, on data about 2-3x shorter than the decoded strings, with no output writes. A filter-only column then never needs decoding. Previous FSST work (simple decode loop, batched decode, rare-pair search, heap reuse) all kept the decode; this removes it.
plan: 1) Plumb filter-only information. Add `bool filter_only = false` to the scan-side filter entry (ScanFilter in src/include/duckdb/storage/table/scan_state.hpp, built by ScanFilterInfo in src/storage/table/scan_state.cpp around :59-102). Set it when the filter's scan_column_index is not in the TableScan projection_ids (table_scan.cpp: g_state->projection_ids at :497/:533 — pass them down at local-state init, or mark in ScanFilterInfo after InitializeScan). In row_group.cpp (:781) set a matching flag on state.column_scans[scan_idx] (new ColumnScanState field) before col_data.Filter. 2) In src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp, add FSSTStorage::Filter (compression_filter_t signature like DictFSSTFilter in dict_fsst.cpp:180) and register it as the function's filter. Inside it: (a) recognise an ExpressionFilter that is optionally NOT(...) over contains(col, const) / ~~ / !~~ with a VARCHAR constant made only of literals and '%' (bail on '_', and on ILIKE/other functions). Mirror the parsing in column_segment.cpp GetSubstringPrefilter:714 and record the start/end anchoring. (b) Build a byte DFA: chained KMP over the literals; dead state for a failed prefix anchor; for an end anchor, accept iff the last literal's KMP state is full at end of string. (c) Per segment symbol table (cache by decoder pointer in the filter state or the FSST scan state), precompute trans[state][code] for codes 0..254 by running the symbol's bytes through the byte DFA; code 255 = escape, so apply the next literal byte. Use the uint8 state type when states <= 255. (d) Walk the compressed strings for the vector, using the same offset and bitunpack logic as StringScanPartial (fsst.cpp:733), and build sel. NULL rows never pass (check validity, same as the prefilter's ROW_NULL handling). (e) Result vector: if the column is filter_only, do not decode. Leave result as a valid placeholder (e.g. a constant empty string), because row_group.cpp:789 Slices it. Otherwise decode only the rows in sel into result (DecodeString, fsst.cpp:576), or decode all if that is simpler. For any unsupported filter, fall back to the current path: scan_vector, then ColumnSegment::FilterSelection. Advance the scan state exactly as the scan would. The StandardColumnData::Filter gates still apply: a validity compression without a filter (columns with NULLs) and partial vectors fall back automatically. 3) Tests: LIKE/NOT LIKE/contains with prefix, suffix, infix and multi-% patterns; strings containing escape-coded bytes; NULLs; a column used both in the filter and in the output; compare against SET disabled_optimizers / a non-FSST copy (TEMP tables are never compressed, so use a persistent table with FORCE compression 'fsst'). Micro A/B on q13 with .timer.
expected_gain: q13 -30..-50%: scan CPU 2.17s -> about 0.6s, with 15M strings at roughly 20 codes each and about 1-2ns per lookup. That is about -3..-5% geomean. q09: p_name contains 'ghost' on a filter-only FSST column, small (part scan 0.11s CPU). Hidden: q16-style s_comment LIKE, q20-style p_name LIKE 'forest%'.
generality: Any LIKE/contains/prefix/suffix scan filter on an FSST-compressed VARCHAR column (comments, names, descriptions); the biggest gains are where the column is only filtered, not output. Nothing changes for Dictionary/DictFSST/uncompressed columns. Possible slowdown: a column that is filtered AND output with a low-selectivity predicate pays the DFA plus the decode of passing rows. That should still be no slower than decode plus prefilter, but verify q13 with o_comment also projected.
risk: Medium-high on correctness: DFA construction, escape codes, end anchoring, NOT/NULL semantics, and scan-state advancement inside a new filter callback. These are contained in fsst.cpp plus a one-bool plumbing change. Wrong results are caught by the pattern tests above. Performance risk is low, because unsupported filters fall back to the current path.

title: FSST code-level LIKE filter v2: DFA over FSST codes + filter-only no-decode + segment-straddling vectors
hypothesis: q13 (313ms, slowest template) spends 2.17s of operator CPU in the orders TABLE_SCAN running o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%'. o_comment is plain FSST, and FSST registers no filter callback, so StandardColumnData::Filter (standard_column_data.cpp:76-94) falls back to decode-all and then filter. The column is filter-only, so TableScan drops the decoded strings afterwards. An implementation earlier in this run (the r10 dispatch: FSSTStorage::Filter + a KMP-chain DFA lifted to codes + a filter_only flag) measured q13 -16..-21% on the bench. EXPLAIN ANALYZE scan CPU went from 1.88s to 1.26s. The DFA itself costs only ~0.45s. About 13% of vectors cross an FSST segment boundary, so GetVectorScanType != SCAN_ENTIRE_VECTOR, and these vectors take the full-decode fallback (~0.25s, about 40% of the remaining non-DFA cost). Handling straddling vectors with the same DFA path should push q13 clearly beyond its ~14% noise band.
plan: 1) Re-implement the earlier version. Add a filter_only flag to ScanFilter (src/include/duckdb/storage/table/scan_state.hpp, set in scan_state.cpp ScanFilterInfo from the TableScan projection_ids in table_scan.cpp) and mirror it into ColumnScanState before col_data.Filter in row_group.cpp (~:781). Add FSSTStorage::Filter in src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp, modelled on DictFSSTFilter (dict_fsst.cpp:180). It parses NOT?(contains|prefix|suffix|~~|!~~) with a constant pattern made only of literals and '%' (bail on '_', ILIKE and escapes) into a byte DFA (KMP chain with anchors). Per segment symbol table (cached by decoder pointer), lift it to a uint16 table trans[state][code] with escape-pending states. Run it over the vector's compressed strings, using the StringScanPartial offset and bitunpack logic, with a 4-way interleave over the lanes. NULL rows never pass. For a filter_only column, emit a constant placeholder and do not decode. Otherwise decode only the rows in sel. Any unsupported filter falls back to the existing path. 2) New in v2: in StandardColumnData::Filter, when the only failing gate is that the vector straddles a segment boundary (no updates, compression->filter on both segments, and validity has a filter or NO_VALIDITY_REQUIRED), filter piecewise. For each segment piece, call the segment's filter for the piece's row count into a temp sel, add the piece's row offset to the sel indices, and append. Advance the data and validity child states across the boundary the way ScanVector/BeginScanVectorInternal does. If that is too invasive, limit it to filter_only columns and skip the result vector entirely. 3) Tests: prefix, suffix, infix and multi-% patterns, NOT, NULLs, escape-coded bytes, a column both filtered and projected, and a vector crossing a segment boundary. Use `col||''` as a no-pushdown reference (dbe-tool sql is read-only).
expected_gain: q13 -20..-28% (previous version -16..-21%, plus the ~0.25s straddle fallback removed), about -1.5..-2% geomean. Hidden templates with LIKE on FSST comment or name columns (q16 s_comment, q20 p_name 'forest%' if it is not turned into a range) gain a few %.
generality: Any LIKE/contains/prefix/suffix scan filter on an FSST-compressed VARCHAR, largest where the column is only filtered. Dictionary, DictFSST and uncompressed columns are unchanged. A filtered-and-projected column with a low-selectivity predicate pays the DFA plus the decode of passing rows, which should be about even.
risk: Medium-high on correctness: DFA escapes, anchors, NOT/NULL semantics, and the piecewise scan-state advance across segments in the straddle path. Performance risk is low, because unsupported cases fall back.

title: FSST DFA filter: lane-refill interleaving + absorbing-state early exit
hypothesis: After E0042, q13 (261ms, 2nd slowest) still spends 1.23s CPU in the orders scan (profile.md). Measured hot with dbe-tool sql: `count(*) WHERE o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%'` takes 172ms wall / 1.35s user, and `NOT LIKE '%zq%'` (a 2-state DFA) takes 161ms. A full FSST decode of all 15M strings is cheaper: `WHERE o_comment <> 'abc'` takes 84ms and `sum(length(o_comment))` 88ms. So the code-level DFA is about 2x slower than decoding, even though it writes nothing. The cause is the loop in FSSTStorage::Filter (fsst.cpp:1114-1151). It groups 4 strings, runs the 4 interleaved chains only up to the SHORTEST length (`common`), then finishes each string's tail serially (`for k = common..lens[l]`). o_comment lengths vary widely (about 19-78 chars, so roughly 8-35 codes), so most codes run on a single dependent chain, `s = table[s + code]`, at about 6 cycles per code (L1 load latency plus the add). That is about 3ns/code, which matches 375M codes / 1.3s. Also, nothing exits early when the DFA reaches an absorbing state (the 'dead' state of a failed anchor, or 'done' when an unanchored-end pattern has matched). So a prefix pattern like 'forest%' or a contains of a common word still walks every code.
plan: Only the inner loop and pattern init in src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp change. (1) In the FSST scan state's pattern initialisation (InitializePattern, around fsst.cpp:768-790, where pattern_table and pattern_accept are built), also compute per state whether it is absorbing: every one of the 256 code transitions, including the escape states, returns to the same state. FSSTPatternDFA::Build already creates explicit `done`/`dead` states (fsst.cpp:654-671), so this can simply be taken from there. Store it as a bit in pattern_accept (for example bit 1), or as a parallel vector indexed by s>>8. (2) Replace the 4-group loop (fsst.cpp:1114-1151) with a K-lane scheduler, K=8 (try 6/8/12). Each lane holds (cur ptr, end ptr, state, row). Each iteration advances every active lane by one code; this is the hot path with independent chains. When a lane reaches its end, or (checked every code or every few codes) enters an absorbing state, record accept for its row and refill the lane from the next candidate in sel. Rows that finish early must still land in new_sel in ascending order. Simplest: write a per-candidate pass/fail byte array indexed by candidate position i, then compact into new_sel in a final loop. Drain the remaining lanes at the end. Keep the escape-code handling exactly as it is now (escape states are ordinary table states, so it is unchanged). (3) Optional, measure separately: a speculative fast path for state 0 of unanchored patterns, `s = s ? table[s+c] : table0[c]`, which breaks the data dependency through branch prediction while the DFA sits in its start state. Micro A/B with .timer: NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%', NOT LIKE '%zq%', LIKE '%unusual%packages%', contains(o_comment,'the'), and prefix-only LIKE 'ab%' on o_comment. Goal: below the 84ms decode baseline. Correctness: compare counts against the `o_comment||''` reference for the same pattern set the E0042 implementer used, including multi-%, anchors, NOT, escape-coded bytes, and candidate rows already narrowed by a previous filter.
expected_gain: q13: the scan accounts for about 170ms of a 261ms query. If the DFA reaches about 2x throughput (1.35s -> about 0.6s CPU), q13 drops to about 190-210ms (-20..-25%), roughly -1.5..-2% geomean. Templates without LIKE on FSST columns: 0.
generality: Every LIKE/NOT LIKE/contains/prefix/suffix scan filter on an FSST VARCHAR column (comments, names, addresses). Early exit helps prefix-anchored patterns most (q20-style p_name LIKE 'forest%': dead after 1-2 codes) and contains on common words. Nothing changes for Dictionary/DictFSST/uncompressed columns. Worst case: very short strings, where lane-refill bookkeeping per string could cost more than it saves; o_comment and p_name are 20-80 chars.
risk: Low-medium. One function plus an init-time flag, with no plan or plumbing changes. Correctness risk: rows reaching new_sel out of order, or lost lane state at the drain. Both are caught by count comparisons against the ||'' reference.

title: FSST DFA filter: SIMD skip of codes that keep an unanchored DFA in state 0
hypothesis: The q13 orders scan (o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%', 15M rows) is still the largest piece of q13 (237ms, 12% of the total). E0043's probes split the count micro query (~160ms) as follows: a floor of ~75ms without the DFA walk, ~25ms for touching the string bytes, and ~60ms for the per-code dependent table walk in FSSTStorage::Filter (fsst.cpp:1115-1151). Adding ILP (8 lanes, rounds, length-sorted groups) did not help, so making each lookup faster is a dead end. The remaining lever is doing fewer lookups. For an unanchored pattern, the DFA sits in state 0 for almost every code. Only codes whose symbol bytes move state 0 to a non-zero state (pattern_table[0 + c] != 0: symbols ending in a prefix of the first literal, plus FSST_ESC=255) can start progress. A 16-code SIMD membership test on a 256-bit 'leaves state 0' set finds the next such code, so the scalar walk runs only from there until it returns to state 0. For rare literals that cuts the scalar lookups by about 5-10x. The walk's ~60ms should drop to ~10-20ms, so q13 falls ~15-20%.
plan: In src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp: (1) In FSSTScanState::InitializePattern (~:771), after building pattern_table, compute a 256-bit set leave0[c] = (pattern_table[c] != 0) for c in 0..255. FSST_ESC always leaves, because it maps to a pending state. Also build pshufb nibble tables: for each low nibble, an 8-bit mask over (hi & 7), with separate tables for hi < 8 and hi >= 8. Set a flag skip_ok = has_pattern && !anchored_start && popcount(leave0) <= 128. Anchored-start patterns already reach a dead state quickly, so leave them alone. To see anchoring, either expose it from FSSTPatternDFA::Build/TryCreate (:551/:622) or derive it as 'state 0 is not reachable from state 0 via some code'. Simplest: skip_ok only if pattern_table[0 + c] == 0 for most c. (2) In FSSTStorage::Filter (:1081), when skip_ok, replace the 4-lane loop with a per-string loop: k = 0; s = 0; loop { if s == 0: find the next k' >= k with leave0[str[k']] using a 16-byte SIMD block test (load 16 bytes, mask off the bits past len, take the first set bit); if none is found, break with s = 0; otherwise k = k'. Then run scalar s = table[s + str[k]]; k++ while s != 0 && k < len }. Accept with accept[s >> 8] as today. The pending-escape states are >= 256*pattern_states and so are non-zero, so the scalar path consumes the escape byte correctly. Reading past the string end: compressed strings sit back to back in the segment dictionary, but the 16-byte load must not cross the end of the block buffer (scan_state.handle.Ptr() + segment block size). Near the end, use a scalar loop over leave0 instead. (3) SIMD portability: use SSSE3 _mm_shuffle_epi8 nibble lookup inside a function with __attribute__((target("ssse3"))) and __builtin_cpu_supports("ssse3") checked once, or #if defined(__SSSE3__). Otherwise use a scalar fallback that tests a 256-byte leave0 flag array. Those flag lookups are independent loads, not a dependent chain, so the fallback is still a win. Check how E0032 / column_segment.cpp included SSE intrinsics and follow the same convention. (4) Test LIKE, NOT LIKE and contains with infix, multi-%, suffix-anchored and prefix-anchored patterns (the prefix-anchored ones keep the old path). Include a pattern whose first byte is common ('%e%'), a pattern matching inside an escape-coded byte, and strings shorter than 16 codes at the block end. Compare counts with the o_comment||'' reference (which disables pushdown). Micro A/B with .timer: count(*) WHERE o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%' (r11 baseline 172ms), NOT LIKE '%zq%' (161ms), contains 'the' (147ms; must not regress).
expected_gain: q13 -10..-20% (scan walk ~60ms of wall time → ~15ms); geomean ~-1..-1.5%. Hidden templates: any LIKE '%lit%' / contains filter on an FSST comment or name column (q16-style s_comment, p_name LIKE '%green%' shapes).
generality: Every unanchored LIKE/contains/NOT LIKE scan filter on an FSST-compressed VARCHAR column. It is an exact rewrite of the same DFA walk, so results are unchanged. It can be slower when the first literal byte is very common (e.g. '%e%', where most codes leave state 0): the popcount gate plus a per-vector fallback would bound that cost. A simple per-vector option: if the scalar step count exceeds about half the codes, switch to the old loop for the rest of the segment.
risk: Medium-low. One file, and the DFA semantics are unchanged. The main bug risks are over-reading past the block buffer and mishandling escape-pending states. The 16-byte tail guard and the reference tests cover both. Performance risk: q13's noise is ~14%, so the change needs to clear that; rerun q13 alone if the result is borderline.

title: Leaner streamed-run store for clustered-key radix agg (q18 subquery)
hypothesis: q18 (236ms, 12% of total) is dominated by the IN-subquery `SELECT l_orderkey FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity) > 312`. The EXPLAIN ANALYZE of this subquery alone gives HASH_GROUP_BY 1.33s CPU over 60M rows into 15M groups, and FILTER 0.06s on 15M rows. Hot-run micro timings (.timer, r13): sum(l_orderkey),sum(l_quantity) scan only 39ms; `select distinct l_orderkey` 133ms; count(l_quantity) group by 165ms; sum(l_quantity) group by 185-195ms; the HAVING version 191-217ms. So about 95ms of wall time is group handling for 15M streamed runs that have no aggregate at all, i.e. about 50ns CPU per group. The aggregate update is only about 20-30ms. E0036 sends interior runs through SinkInteriorRuns (radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:718). For every input chunk it allocates one arena block of states per run, fills a 2048-entry address vector, calls RowOperations::InitializeStates and UpdateStates per aggregate plus AddInPlace, Slices the keys by run heads (a dictionary vector), and Appends (key, row-pointer) to a ColumnDataCollection, which copies. The source side (around :1554-1585) then scans the CDC, gathers the states through the pointers in FinalizeStates, and Outputs 15M rows. These are several passes and copies for each group, which is where the per-group cost goes.
plan: Measure first (about 30 min). Add temporary timers, or use perf if available, around the parts of SinkInteriorRuns (FindRunHeads, state allocation and address fill, InitializeStates, UpdateStates, CDC Append) and around the run-store source path (Scan, FinalizeStates, Output), using the distinct and the sum micro queries above. Then fix the dominant part with one mechanism. Preferred: replace the per-local-state ColumnDataCollection run store with a plain append-only list of fixed-size blocks per thread. Each block holds a column of run keys (memcpy of the head keys, no dictionary slice and no CDC) and the aggregate states for those runs, contiguous and in the same order, so that no row-pointer column is needed and the states are addressed by index. Initialize the states of a whole block in one InitializeStates call. In the source, finalize a block's states in vector-sized slices straight into the output chunk, using a row-pointer vector computed arithmetically rather than stored. Keep the MergeRunStores fallback (used when intervals overlap) working on the new blocks. Do not change when streaming is used. If the measurement shows the cost is downstream (Output plus the decompress projection and FILTER over 15M rows) rather than in the store, report that and stop rather than guess. Abandon if the q18 micro does not improve by at least 8%.
expected_gain: q18 -5..-12% (cutting the ~95ms of group handling by a third or more on a ~195ms subquery); geomean about -0.5..-1%
generality: Any GROUP BY whose first key is clustered in storage order with many small groups: order-level rollups of line tables, GROUP BY on a sort or insert key, time-series per-id aggregation. Queries whose keys are not clustered never take this path. Possible slowdown: the fallback merge when intervals overlap (q03-like) must stay as cheap as now.
risk: Medium. State lifetime and destructors for non-trivial aggregate states (lists, strings) must still run once; the fallback merge must see the same states. Test with string_agg/list aggregates on clustered keys, with overlapping intervals (unsorted input), and with HAVING.

title: Eager pre-aggregation below a dimension join that only supplies group keys (q09 n_name)
hypothesis: In q09 the final GROUP BY n_name, o_year runs on 3.27M join rows with a string key: the string is carried through the supplier⋈nation build side, compressed to uhugeint (0.08s CPU) and hashed (HASH_GROUP_BY 0.20s CPU). Hot micro timings (r13), q09 with count(*): GROUP BY n_name,year 247-251ms; GROUP BY n_nationkey,year 211-224ms; so the string key costs about 30ms, about 10% of q09 (313ms, the largest template). Grouping first on (s_nationkey, o_year) below the nation join, then joining 175 partial groups to nation and re-aggregating by (n_name, o_year), avoids carrying and hashing the string for 3.27M rows. This is valid for decomposable aggregates (SUM, COUNT as SUM of counts, MIN, MAX) without any uniqueness constraint, because every original row is multiplied by the same number of matches either way.
plan: Optimizer rule after join ordering (src/optimizer/, new pass or inside an existing aggregate pass; verify where the final join tree is available). Pattern: AGGREGATE(groups G, decomposable aggs A) over a chain of INNER joins whose top join (or one hop below) joins a small build-side relation R (estimated cardinality < ~1000) on an equality key k, where R contributes only group columns and none of the aggregate inputs. Rewrite to AGG2(G, combine(A)) over JOIN(AGG1(G minus R's columns, plus k; A), R). Only fire when AGG1's estimated groups are much smaller than its input (for example 10x). Needs care with the CM projections and column bindings. Test: TPC-H q05/q07/q09-style queries against SET disabled_optimizers for the new rule, NULL keys, and duplicate keys in R.
expected_gain: q09 -8..-12%; q05/q07 small (their aggregate inputs are only 100K-1M rows)
generality: Star-schema queries that group by dimension attributes (names or regions) over large fact joins, which is very common. It could slow queries where the pre-aggregation does not reduce rows (gate on the estimate).
risk: High: a new optimizer rewrite with binding and CM interactions, and the join tree may not put the dimension join at the top. Dispatch only if a contained change is not available.

title: Template-copy aggregate state initialization for destructor-free layouts
hypothesis: RowOperations::InitializeStates (src/common/row_operations/row_aggregate.cpp:8) calls aggr.function.GetStateInitCallback() indirectly once per state per aggregate. The E0045 implementer measured it at ~62-72ms CPU for q18's HAVING subquery (15M streamed runs). That makes it the third-largest per-group cost after the address fill (93ms) and UpdateStates (112ms). q18 is 180ms, the #3 template. The same function also initializes every new group in GroupedAggregateHashTable (FindOrCreateGroups), so every high-cardinality hash aggregate pays one indirect call per group per aggregate. For layouts with no destructor (!layout.HasDestructor()), the initialized state bytes are the same for every row. Initializing one template block and copying it with memcpy turns N*A indirect calls into A calls plus N fixed-size copies.
plan: In src/common/row_operations/row_aggregate.cpp, RowOperations::InitializeStates: if !layout.HasDestructor() and count >= some small threshold (e.g. 4), use a template block. Allocate it once with GetAggrWidth() bytes; a thread_local or stack buffer is fine for widths <= 256 bytes, otherwise use the old path. Zero it. Run each aggregate's init callback once on template + (offsets[aggr_idx] - layout.GetAggrOffset()). Then, for each row i (through sel if set), memcpy(pointers[idx] + GetAggrOffset(), template, aggr_width). Specialize the copy loop for common widths (8/16/24/32/48/64 via a templated fixed-size memcpy) so it is not a libc call per row. Keep the old loop when there are destructors. Check that the aggregate offsets are contiguous from GetAggrOffset (tuple_data_layout.hpp:86-90); if any offset falls outside [aggr_offset, aggr_offset+aggr_width), fall back. Tests: the aggregate test suite (sum/avg/min/max/count/bit_and/arg_min/first, decimal and hugeint sums), q18 results, and GROUP BY with FILTER. Measure the q18 HAVING micro with .timer (baseline 136-143ms) and the full bench.
expected_gain: q18 -3..-6% (≈60ms CPU of the subquery's per-group cost). Small gains on other many-group hash aggregates (q03, q16, q09 partial aggregates, q18's main HT). Geomean ~-0.5..-1%.
generality: Every grouped hash aggregate whose states have no destructor (sum/count/min/max/avg over numerics, which is most analytic GROUP BYs). Gains grow with the number of groups. List/string_agg/holistic aggregates keep the old path. Few-group aggregates do one extra template init per call, which is negligible.
risk: Low. The one assumption is that the init callbacks write address-independent bytes. That holds for destructor-free states because they hold no owned pointers, and the gate excludes the rest. A contained, single-function diff.

title: q18 clustered agg bundle: batched run-interval registration + template state init
hypothesis: After E0045 the q18 HAVING subquery (60M rows, ~29K chunks, 15M runs) spends ~69ms CPU (summed over threads) in RegisterRunInterval (radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:813). It takes a global mutex and does a std::map insert per chunk, which is ~2.4us per chunk, so most of it is lock contention across 8 threads. It also spends 62-72ms in RowOperations::InitializeStates (row_aggregate.cpp:8), one indirect call per state for 15M states. E0046 (template-copy init alone) measured q18 ~-2%, inside the 5% noise. Batching the interval registration (one lock per 64 chunks) removes most of the contention. Combined with template init, that should take ~100ms CPU (~12ms wall of ~178ms) off q18, enough to clear noise.
plan: 1) radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp: give RadixHTLocalSinkState a small pending-interval buffer (vector<pair<uint64_t,uint64_t>>, cap 64). In SinkClustered (:934), instead of calling RegisterRunInterval per chunk, first check the local buffer for overlap with the new interval, then append it. When the buffer is full, and always in Combine/before finalize (wherever lstate.intervals and the run stores are handed to gstate), flush: take run_intervals_lock once, check and insert every pending interval (same lower_bound/prev logic), and set run_intervals_overlap on any conflict. Keep the exact open-interval endpoints: do NOT merge (a,b),(b,c) into (a,c), because another thread's interval starting at boundary key b would look like a false overlap. Required correctness check: overlap is now detected up to 64 chunks late, after those runs were already streamed. Confirm that the overlap path (run_intervals_overlap -> MergeRunStores ~:989 / run source :1554) already routes streamed run stores through the normal combine when overlap is set. Today an overlap found by RegisterRunInterval already happens after earlier intervals were streamed, so this should hold; if it does not, add the fallback. Every flush must finish before any finalize reads run_intervals_overlap. 2) Re-apply the E0046 template-copy init in row_aggregate.cpp RowOperations::InitializeStates: for layouts where no aggregate has a destructor, and init does not depend on the address, initialize one template state block once (cache it on the layout or the HT), then memcpy it to each row's aggregate offset. Keep the per-aggregate path otherwise. 3) Tests: the clustered-agg tests, plus a test where two threads' chunks overlap late (e.g. a union of two sorted ranges), checked against SET disabled clustered path / a shuffled copy. A/B q18 with .timer (sum of 8 subqueries).
expected_gain: q18 -4..-7% (~-0.5% geomean). Other GROUP BYs with many groups get a small gain from template init.
generality: Any GROUP BY over input clustered on the first key (sorted/insert-ordered FK columns), and any hash aggregate creating many groups with destructor-free states (SUM/COUNT/MIN/MAX on numerics). Possible slowdown: input that overlaps late now streams up to 64 more chunks before it falls back.
risk: Medium-low. The delayed overlap detection must be covered by the existing fallback, and the template memcpy must skip aggregates whose init is not a plain constant fill.

title: Leaner staged sink for large perfect HA: no local table + fused typed scatter
hypothesis: q13 (226ms, #2 template) spends about 0.43s profile CPU (roughly 0.11s real) in PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY (Large Table) over 15.3M join rows into 2^21 slots. In the shared staged path (E0034), two costs do no useful work. (1) Each thread's local PerfectAggregateHashTable (perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp ctor :34-53, lazy_init) still allocates tuple_size*total_groups bytes it never writes, and memsets a 2MB lazy_group_is_set array. The memset page-faults about 500 4K pages per thread, plus the large malloc and free churn. Once SetStageTarget returns true, all updates go to the target HT. (2) AddChunkStaged (:257-318) first counting-sorts the rows into sorted_rows/sorted_slots, then calls VectorOperations::Copy once per stripe per payload column. That is 32 stripes, so about 32 generic Copy calls of about 64 rows each per chunk, roughly 234K calls for q13, each going through the generic type and validity dispatch. A second pass that writes each row straight to its final stage-buffer position (typed for flat fixed-width payloads) removes both the sorted_rows indirection and the per-call overhead.
plan: 1) perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp/.hpp: let the lazy-init constructor defer allocating owned_data and lazy_group_is_set until first non-staged use. Add a private EnsureLocalStorage() called from UpdateLazy when target==*this, from CombineRange/Combine when this table is the target, and from any scan/finalize path. Grep every use of data, lazy_group_is_set and owned_data and guard them. Simplest correct option: allocate lazily in AddChunkLazy when !use_staging, in FlushStagePartition when stage_target==nullptr, and in the global HT's first use. Destroy() must handle data==nullptr. Check that the global HT (gstate.ht) still allocates before the first concurrent FlushStagePartition, either by allocating eagerly for the global table (it is created by CreateHT in PerfectHashAggregateGlobalState) or through a flag, so no race. 2) AddChunkStaged: before the scatter, make sure every partition's current buffer has room for its count (do the same advance/flush logic up front per partition). Then, for payload columns that are flat (or ToUnifiedFormat with a sel) and of a constant-size physical type, do one typed loop over i in 0..count: pos = offsets[p]++; write value and validity to buffers[p].data[c][base_p+pos], and the slot to buffers[p].slots. Keep the current Copy path for other vector types. Put the type dispatch in a small templated helper (int32/int64/hugeint/double etc.; fall back to Copy otherwise). 3) Verify q13 results against SET disabled_optimizers or the small-table path. Micro A/B: q13 with .timer, runs 2+, 8 threads. Also check q01-style perfect HA (non-large) is unchanged.
expected_gain: q13 -2..-5% (the perfect HA is about 6% of q13 wall, the local table setup about 1-2%). Probably inside q13's 14% noise; this is the last low-risk item for that template.
generality: Every large-range perfect hash aggregate (GROUP BY on dense FK keys up to 2^22 groups), which is common for per-customer, per-part and per-supplier counts. Small perfect HA and radix HA are untouched. No template should get slower: memory and work only go down.
risk: Low-medium. Lazy allocation must not race when the global HT is first used from several threads (allocate the global table eagerly). The typed scatter must copy validity correctly for NULL payloads (RIGHT-join unmatched rows have a NULL o_orderkey, and count must skip them).
